title: Global challenges, local responses: Exploring curriculum reform in South African engineering education
text_snippet: Global challenges, local responses: Exploring curriculum reform in South African engineering education Abstract Background and Aim There have been significant higher education curriculum reform initiatives over the past 30 years across different global regions in response to a range of drivers such as employability, global citizenship, and sustainability. In professions such as engineering, a key focus has been on holistic graduate attribute development for scarce skills needs in increasingly complex socio‐technical sectors. This paper sets out to explore the drivers of engineering curriculum reform in higher education institutions (HEIs) in a Global South context. Design/Method Drawing on semi‐structured, recorded focus group interviews with 28 program coordinators and academics across 15 of the 16 HEIs offering engineering qualifications in South Africa, the research team set out to determine what kinds of curriculum reform initiatives were being undertaken, who was responsible for initiating, implementing, and supporting these initiatives, and what were perceived to be challenges and successes. The emergent drivers were framed in relation to curriculum responsiveness theory analyzed using an overarching “critical realist” framework with structure, culture, and agency dimensions that systemically influence how curriculum reform is constrained or enabled. title: Collaboration rules: A narrative comparison of engineering students and practicing engineers' collaboration experiences and beliefs using structuration theory
text_snippet: Collaboration rules: A narrative comparison of engineering students and practicing engineers' collaboration experiences and beliefs using structuration theory Abstract Background Collaboration—including coordination, communication, and teamwork—is crucial to engineering practice. However, engineering students are often perceived as lacking key collaboration skills at the time of graduation. Purpose We used structuration theory to explore how differences between students and practitioners' collaboration beliefs related to differences between academic and professional collaboration contexts. We sought to demonstrate that the perceived collaboration “skill gap” in engineering students can be explained by differences between academic and professional social systems. Methods We conducted interviews with 30 undergraduate engineering students and 28 practicing engineers, and from these interviews produced 98 discrete narratives of participants' collaboration experiences. We thematically analyzed these 98 collaboration narratives to identify student and practitioner collaboration beliefs. We further coded four narratives for organizational enablements and constraints to show how differences in student and practitioner collaboration beliefs related to differences in organizational collaboration “rules.” Findings Students described boosting productivity through teamwork and limiting soci

title: Exploring supports for belonging as predictors of student outcomes: Different roles of co‐curricular and extracurricular activities in engineering by students' year in college
text_snippet: Exploring supports for belonging as predictors of student outcomes: Different roles of co‐curricular and extracurricular activities in engineering by students' year in college Abstract Background Although most engineering colleges offer a variety of co‐curricular and extracurricular activities to enrich students' sense of belonging to the college, existing literature has not fully captured whether and how the various activities serve to support students' sense of belonging and predict student outcomes. Purpose We investigated how engineering students perceive diverse activities as supports for their sense of belonging, and how these perceptions predict their engineering motivation, persistence, and achievement depending on their year in college. Method Five thousand eleven first‐ to fourth‐year students from the College of Engineering of a four‐year, public university participated in a longitudinal, multicohort study. They reported their engineering‐related motivation, persistence, and perceptions about the extent to which four types of activities (i.e., university programs; college programs; co‐ops/internships and course teamwork; student organizations and research) contributed to their sense of belonging (i.e., served as supports for belonging). title: Transitioning into engineering education: Diverse pathways of military veterans
text_snippet: Transitioning into engineering education: Diverse pathways of military veterans Abstract Background In the United States, there is increased demand to expand the engineering workforce. Many military veterans have received technical training that can be leveraged in engineering. Their pursuit of engineering degrees has great potential to expand and diversify the engineering workforce. Purpose This study examines the pathways of US military veterans from high school graduation through undergraduate engineering education and explores the resources they use to navigate their transition into engineering study. Methods Applying Schlossberg's transition model, this multimethod study uses semi‐structured interviews of 28 student veterans in engineering (SVEs) across four universities. Illustrative examples integrate thematic analyses of interview data and path analysis of key event timeline data. Results Path diagrams illustrate that SVEs embark on diverse pathways and engage in multiple transitions across high school graduation, military training, and undergraduate engineering education. Military experiences, especially engineering‐related work, and encouragement from military supervisors, other veterans, and family contribute to SVEs' pursuit of engineering degrees. title: Exploring engagement narratives among self‐identified Hispanic women's experiences in engineering counterspaces
text_snippet: Exploring engagement narratives among self‐identified Hispanic women's experiences in engineering counterspaces Abstract Background Diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts in higher education are increasingly recognizing the importance of understanding students' lived experience. More research is needed to deeply and contextually uncover voices, meanings, and stories that are enveloped within the complex realities of Hispanic women in engineering. Purpose While the Latiné/x/a/o, Hispanic women population is one of the fastest growing ethnic groups in the United States, they receive only 3% of engineering undergraduate degrees. This research explored how self‐identified Hispanic women experienced engagement outside of class. Design/Method This exploratory qualitative research employed narrative inquiry design using a paradigmatic analysis method. We conducted two in‐depth interviews with five undergraduate engineering students who self‐identified as international Hispanic women. Findings By examining the narratives through a novel synthesis of a socio‐ecological framework of engagement and community cultural wealth, we identified three themes that tell the story of students' experiences outside of class: (i) Perceived benefits and level of involvement informed student dispositions and aspirational capital in counterspaces; (ii) Linguistic capital served as the entry point for r

title: Intercultural Education in Chinese University EFL Classrooms: Intercultural Communication Competence Profiles and the Predictive Roles of Teacher–Student Rapport and Classroom Engagement
text_snippet: Intercultural Education in Chinese University EFL Classrooms: Intercultural Communication Competence Profiles and the Predictive Roles of Teacher–Student Rapport and Classroom Engagement ABSTRACT Intercultural communication competence (ICC) is increasingly regarded as an important goal of intercultural education in university EFL classrooms, where students are expected to engage with diverse perspectives and communicate across cultural boundaries. However, previous research has often examined ICC through variable‐centred approaches, paying limited attention to how different ICC dimensions combine within individual learners and how classroom conditions differentiate students' intercultural development. To address this gap, the present study adopted a person‐centred approach to identify latent ICC profiles among Chinese university students in EFL settings and to examine whether teacher‐student rapport (TSR) and classroom engagement (CE) predicted profile membership. A total of 812 students from a comprehensive university in China participated in the study. Latent profile analysis identified five distinct ICC profiles: Overall‐Low, Relatively Balanced, Awareness‐Prominent, Reflective‐Imbalanced, and Comprehensively High. Multinomial logistic regression showed that both TSR and CE significantly contributed to the prediction of profile membership, although CE displayed a more consis

title: Exploring the Mediation of EFL Learners' Perceptions of Teacher Fairness on the Association Between Learning Climate and Self‐Efficacy
text_snippet: Exploring the Mediation of EFL Learners' Perceptions of Teacher Fairness on the Association Between Learning Climate and Self‐Efficacy ABSTRACT Self‐efficacy refers to the learners' beliefs in their abilities to adjust their learning, which can lead to learners' educational success and motivation, and thus, is important within the learning procedure. The learning climate has a vital effect on the educational performance, especially within the English language learning sphere. Moreover, teachers' behaviour in the classroom affects the students' performance, and among those behaviours, fairness dominates others because practitioners and researchers have been interested in practicing and researching fairness. Teachers' fair behaviour within the class enhances students' emotional and academic feelings. The present research investigated the effect of learning climate on the EFL learners' self‐efficacy, which investigated the mediating effect of teacher fairness in the relationship. Consequently, 691 students out of 758 in three Chinese universities took part and completed the three questionnaires. The results through Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) indicated that both learning climate and teacher fairness significantly predicted EFL students' self‐efficacy and teacher fairness significantly mediated the relationship between learning climate and self‐efficacy. title: The Interaction of Authentic Leadership With Organizational Change Readiness
text_snippet: The Interaction of Authentic Leadership With Organizational Change Readiness ABSTRACT This study investigates how authentic leadership (AL) contributes to organizational change readiness in higher education, with particular attention to the relationships among selected dimensions of authentic leadership, change efficacy, and change commitment within a Sino‐foreign university. Drawing on authentic leadership theory and organizational change readiness theory, this study focuses on two established dimensions of authentic leadership, self‐awareness (SA) and internalized moral perspective (IMP), and examines how they interact with change efficacy (CE) and change commitment (CC). Using an explanatory mixed‐methods approach, the research integrates quantitative partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM) with qualitative thematic analysis to examine organizational change within a Sino‐foreign higher education institution. The findings indicate that self‐awareness positively influences change efficacy, which subsequently strengthens change commitment. Additionally, change commitment was positively associated with internalized moral perspective, suggesting that employees' commitment to organizational change reinforces ethical engagement during organizational transformation. title: Influence of Audience, Performing Conditions and Mental Health on Music Performance Anxiety: A Mediated‐Moderated Model
text_snippet: Influence of Audience, Performing Conditions and Mental Health on Music Performance Anxiety: A Mediated‐Moderated Model ABSTRACT Music performance anxiety (MPA) is one of the prevalent issues for musicians' socio‐emotional well‐being. However, research is scarce on how different psychological aspects influence novice musicians' MPA. Following Folkman's cognitive appraisal theory, this study examines how audience reaction influences MPA, with the mediating role of music performing conditions (MPCs) and the moderating role of their mental health (MH) in live performances in the Chinese context. The research design of the current quantitative study was a cross‐sectional survey. Data were collected from 270 final‐year music students in Beijing using a questionnaire. The participants (novice musicians) were recruited using a simple random sampling technique. The regression results revealed that audience reaction strongly predicts MPA ( R 2 = 0.91); MPCs had a weak and non‐significant mediating effect ( B = 0.06, p = 0.056), while their MH had a significant direct effect with no moderating role. These findings suggest that audience‐related factors are more critical than contextual conditions. The study highlights the need for training programmes to help novice musicians manage audience pressure and improve psychological readiness.

title: Serving More Than Food: Teachers' Perceptions of School Meals From a Socio‐Ecological Perspective
text_snippet: Serving More Than Food: Teachers' Perceptions of School Meals From a Socio‐Ecological Perspective ABSTRACT This study examines Turkish teachers' perceptions of school meal provision, using a socio‐ecological perspective as a conceptual lens. Data were collected from 232 teachers, and exploratory factor analysis identified a six‐factor structure: school climate and student well‐being, food quality and hygiene, social equity and family support, stigma and selective implementation, physical and logistical conditions and educational contributions. Descriptive findings indicated generally positive perceptions of psychosocial and educational contributions, alongside more cautious evaluations of food quality, infrastructure and selective provision. Comparative analyses showed that perceptions varied across school contexts, particularly by boarding student status, whereas transported student status was associated specifically with the stigma and selective implementation dimension. Hierarchical regression analyses further indicated that transported and boarding student status added explanatory value beyond school levels. Overall, the findings provide perception‐based evidence that school meals in Türkiye are viewed as educationally and socially meaningful, while also drawing attention to concerns related to quality, logistics and implementation.

title: Localising Inclusion: Pre‐Service Teachers' Attitudes and Conceptualisations in Germany and Russia
text_snippet: Localising Inclusion: Pre‐Service Teachers' Attitudes and Conceptualisations in Germany and Russia ABSTRACT This study examines pre‐service teachers' (PSTs) attitudes towards inclusive education in Germany and Russia and investigates how they relate to teacher training curricula and teacher educators' discourse. A mixed‐methods design was used, including an online survey of PSTs ( n = 460) with an open‐ended question, curriculum review and exploratory interviews with university educators in both contexts. The two samples showed non‐equivalent attitudinal structures: the three‐factor structure supported in Germany did not replicate in Russia. Analysis of open‐ended responses demonstrated that German PSTs predominantly expressed a general individualised understanding of inclusion, while Russian PSTs tended to follow placement‐ and disability‐orientated definitions of inclusion. The findings suggest that inclusion is not interpreted uniformly across contexts but relates to national policy legacies, curricular traditions and teacher education discourses. Teacher education institutions should support PSTs in critically analysing both local and global definitions of inclusion and their implications for their future school practice.

title: AI ‐Driven Instruction and Its Influence on EFL Learners' Self‐Efficacy, Self‐Regulation, and Grit
text_snippet: AI ‐Driven Instruction and Its Influence on EFL Learners' Self‐Efficacy, Self‐Regulation, and Grit ABSTRACT Incorporating AI into language education has shaped new opportunities to increase learners' psychological resources; however, evidence on how AI‐driven instruction influences key traits such as self‐efficacy, self‐regulation and grit remains limited. To address this gap, the present research examined the effect of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) teaching intervention on these constructs among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. To this end, 123 Chinese EFL learners were selected and assigned to experimental and control groups and received the same syllabus content within 10 weeks. The two groups received the same syllabus material, but the experimental group engaged with an AI Chabot that offered adaptive learning support, customized encouragement and immediate feedback. On the contrary, the control group received conventional teacher‐centred teaching through a traditional context. Pre‐ and post‐intervention assessments measured variations in learners' self‐efficacy, self‐regulation and grit. Results from running one‐way Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) indicated that the AI Chabot intervention significantly enhanced learners' psychological traits compared to traditional instruction. Indeed, these findings confirm that AI‐driven instruction substantially improved

title: Parental Support for Chinese Young Students' EFL Learning: A Perspective of Socio‐Economic Status
text_snippet: Parental Support for Chinese Young Students' EFL Learning: A Perspective of Socio‐Economic Status ABSTRACT Previous research has examined the link between parental support and their children's learning achievement, but knowledge of how parental support is influenced by their socio‐economic status (SES) is limited. Using an open‐ended questionnaire and semi‐structured interview, this study investigated primary school students' perceptions of parental support for their English as a foreign language (EFL) learning in a Chinese context and then examined the data from the perspective of SES. The participants were 20 primary six school students selected from two primary schools located in distinctly different SES areas within a city. They completed the questionnaire and interview regarding parental support for their EFL learning. The findings show that high‐SES and low‐SES parents exhibited different support practices for their children's English learning in four aspects: parental monitoring, offering academic assistance, providing affective support, and supplying material support. A deep analysis of the data reveals that these disparities could be associated with four factors in parents' SES: educational level, profession, financial resources, and beliefs about English education.

title: Humanising Web‐Based Learning for Academically Transitioning Students Through Their Voices
text_snippet: Humanising Web‐Based Learning for Academically Transitioning Students Through Their Voices ABSTRACT Web‐based learning (WBL) has been widely used to support students' learning and has demonstrated its role in boosting students' academic success. Little research has focused on strategies that students can use to humanise this mode of learning, especially academically transitioning students. To fill this gap, this study explores the pedagogical use of student voice to humanise WBL during students' academic transition. Informed by a qualitative case study approach, the study involved a group of female students ( N = 12) from a university in China who were academically transitioning to content‐based English reading learning while participating in WBL for out‐of‐class learning. During their semester‐long learning, data were collected naturalistically, including student‐instructor dialogues as well as the students' written reflections and interviews with the students as ways of eliciting their voices. No additional interventions were made. By mainly employing inductive thematic analysis of data sources, the study shows that over time, voice‐making seemed to empower students to agentively participate in learning, reflect upon their learning, and offer critical insights into their interaction between WBL and the constraints on their academic transition. Their voice‐making, coupled with

title: ‘Strong in Will but Weak in Power’: University Teachers' Perceived Values and Pedagogical Approaches to Values Education
text_snippet: ‘Strong in Will but Weak in Power’: University Teachers' Perceived Values and Pedagogical Approaches to Values Education ABSTRACT This qualitative study investigated university teachers' value perceptions and pedagogical approaches to values education. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews, classroom observations and document analysis with 10 Chinese university teachers, the study identified five main value types emphasised by the participants (i.e., benevolence, security, tradition, conformity and self‐direction values) and three approaches adopted in values education (i.e., traditional, constructivist and critical approaches). The findings show that university teachers actively incorporated curricular values into their teaching and enacted these values through their own interpretations and pedagogical decisions. However, their practices displayed an imbalanced pedagogical pattern, characterised by relatively extensive content knowledge but less developed pedagogical content knowledge related to values education. These findings further highlight teachers' struggling agency in a standardised accountability context, where insufficient professional support constrained their capacity to enact values education in pedagogically meaningful ways. The study offers implications for values education reform and teacher development in higher education institutions.

title: Researching Children's Literature Otherwise to Decolonise Childhoods in Experimental Curriculum
text_snippet: Researching Children's Literature Otherwise to Decolonise Childhoods in Experimental Curriculum ABSTRACT This article explores children's literature as a tool for decolonising childhood and curriculum through experimental reading practices. Based on post‐qualitative enquiry, and grounded in decolonial, feminist, and posthumanist theories, the study analyses two reading encounters with children using picturebooks from Global South. These experiences gave rise to assemblages in which children's agency emerged through relationality and entanglements with books, bodies, materialities, and spaces. We argue that literature and childhood, which is often subject to adult norms, can facilitate plural and situated readings that affirm children's worldviews and knowledge. This approach interrogates the conventional and universalist conceptualisations of childhood and reveals possibilities for reimagining the experimental curriculum as a relational and co‐creative space. The article promotes an epistemic and ethical reconstruction of research with children that decentres adult frameworks and expand new possibilities for children's subjectivities and knowledges.

title: Developmental Model of Academic Resilience: A Mixed‐Methods Study
text_snippet: Developmental Model of Academic Resilience: A Mixed‐Methods Study ABSTRACT The purpose of the study is to holistically identify the protective factors that contribute to students' academic resilience and examine the mediating role of protective factors between school burnout and school attachment using an exploratory sequential mixed‐methods design, one of the mixed‐methods research designs. A phenomenological research method was used to reveal the protective factors of students who were able to show academic resilience despite various negative life events. Results show that the factors contributing to academic resilience are categorized as the subthemes of individual, family, school and environmental resources. The mediating role of academic resilience resources in the relationship between school burnout and school attachment was examined using a structural equation model. The results show that resilience resources play a mediating role between school burnout and school attachment.

title: The Evolution of China–Africa Higher Education Cooperation: An Integrative Review for Promising Future Directions
text_snippet: The Evolution of China–Africa Higher Education Cooperation: An Integrative Review for Promising Future Directions ABSTRACT Over the past 20 years, the cooperation between China and Africa in higher education has shifted from mainly providing scholarships to a broader partnership model. This model encompasses academic mobility, institutional collaboration, research networks, vocational education and digital transformation. Despite the rapid growth and increasing importance of these initiatives, understanding how they work, their impact on institutions, their sustainability implications, and their long‐term potential remains limited. This review brings together 39 pieces of evidence from English and Chinese academic literature, policy papers, institutional reports and collaborative frameworks. It critically looks at how higher education cooperation has developed under the Forum on China–Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) from 2006 to the most recent 2024 framework. The review explores four connected areas: the growth and variety of FOCAC‐driven higher education initiatives, their effects on African higher education systems, the challenges to their sustainability, and ways for future cooperation. title: Family SES , Shadow Education and Education‐Related Worry in Suzhou, China: Tutoring and Parental Involvement as Linked Mediators
text_snippet: Family SES , Shadow Education and Education‐Related Worry in Suzhou, China: Tutoring and Parental Involvement as Linked Mediators ABSTRACT Parental educational anxiety is increasingly visible in competitive education systems, but less is known about how family resources may be linked to both lower and higher worry. Using a 2020 parent survey from Suzhou, China ( N = 91,967), this study examines how family socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with parents' education‐related worry through extracurricular tutoring intensity and parental involvement. Educational anxiety is measured as a 10‐item parent‐reported worry scale, not as clinical anxiety. Serial mediation analyses show an inconsistent pattern: SES had negative total and direct associations with educational anxiety, but was positively associated with tutoring intensity and parental involvement, both of which were positively associated with anxiety. Positive indirect pathways through tutoring, involvement, and their sequence partly offset the negative direct association. Although the serial indirect effect was small, it was consistent across robustness checks. The findings show the emotional ambivalence of family advantage in shadow education.

title: Embedding, Copilot, or Agent? L2 Teachers Modes of Collaboration With Generative AI in Providing Feedback on Writing Assignments: Rubric Influences, Workload Dynamics, and Barriers to Integration
text_snippet: Embedding, Copilot, or Agent? L2 Teachers Modes of Collaboration With Generative AI in Providing Feedback on Writing Assignments: Rubric Influences, Workload Dynamics, and Barriers to Integration ABSTRACT Drawing from the established human‐AI collaboration framework (Mosqueira‐Rey et al., 2023), this study investigated how L2 teachers at a research‐intensive university collaborated with Generative AI chatbots to provide feedback on tertiary‐level written assignments over 9 weeks. Data from thirteen teachers included 278 interactions with GenAI, 876 feedback instances, and reflective accounts of their experiences. Findings revealed three Teacher‐GenAI collaboration modes— embedding (human‐led), copilot (interactive), and agent (GenAI‐led)—with a MANOVA indicating that rubric dimensions significantly influenced their frequency of use. Post hoc comparisons indicated that teachers used the agent and copilot modes more frequently in the “language use” dimension. Conversely, the embedding mode was used most frequently in the “content” and “overall evaluation” dimensions. Although the a gent mode reduced teachers' workload in providing feedback on mistakes at the micro level, the embedding mode demanded more effort from teachers to give feedback at the macro level of students' assignments. title: Pulling the Lever Without Moving the Machine: English Teacher Education and the Limits of Sexuality Education Reform
text_snippet: Pulling the Lever Without Moving the Machine: English Teacher Education and the Limits of Sexuality Education Reform ABSTRACT In this paper we draw on complex adaptive systems ( CAS ) theory to explore how changing systems of teacher education constrain attempts to introduce expanded sexuality education curricula. We report findings from a mixed methods study of teacher educators' perceptions of their provision in relation to England's statutory Relationships, Sex and Health Education ( RSHE ) curriculum. Despite its statutory status, RSHE remains unevenly and inconsistently embedded across initial teacher education programmes. We argue that sexuality education reform is unlikely to succeed without matched, sustained investment in teacher education—and that without this, statutory curricula risk generating new negative feedback loops rather than lasting change. We discuss implications for how policymakers might design more systemically coherent approaches to sexuality education reform.

title: From Environment to Engagement: Innovative Insights Into AI ‐Mediated Language Learning Through Psychological Mechanisms
text_snippet: From Environment to Engagement: Innovative Insights Into AI ‐Mediated Language Learning Through Psychological Mechanisms ABSTRACT AI is increasingly used in language learning, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying student engagement remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates the associations among teacher enthusiasm, learner growth mindset, and student engagement in AI‐mediated language learning, with a focus on the mediating roles of willingness to communicate, resilience and creative self‐efficacy. A total of 699 university students participated in a cross‐sectional survey, and the data were analysed using structural equation modelling and psychological network analysis to examine indirect pathways and networked associations among environmental, cognitive and psychological factors. The results indicate that higher levels of teacher enthusiasm and stronger growth mindset are positively associated with psychological variables, which in turn are linked to higher engagement. Network analysis further reveals that willingness to communicate, resilience and creative self‐efficacy are interconnected, with engagement occupying a central position within the network. title: The Effects of AI‐Powered Genre‐Based Writing Instruction on Low‐Proficiency EFL Writers' Ideal L2 Writing Self, Writing Enjoyment and L2 Writing Performance: A Quasi‐Experimental Mixed‐Methods Study
text_snippet: The Effects of AI‐Powered Genre‐Based Writing Instruction on Low‐Proficiency EFL Writers' Ideal L2 Writing Self, Writing Enjoyment and L2 Writing Performance: A Quasi‐Experimental Mixed‐Methods Study ABSTRACT This mixed‐methods study examined the effects of DeepSeek‐powered genre‐based instruction (GBI) on argumentative writing performance, ideal L2 writing self, and writing enjoyment among 71 low‐proficiency EFL undergraduates. A quasi‐experimental design was employed, with an experimental group ( N = 32) receiving 6 weeks of AI‐powered GBI and a control group ( N = 39) receiving traditional instruction. Quantitative data included writing tests (holistic and CAF indices) and motivation questionnaires, while qualitative data came from semi‐structured interviews. title: Immersive Learning in Business Education: The Impact of Metaverse Technology
text_snippet: Immersive Learning in Business Education: The Impact of Metaverse Technology ABSTRACT Metaverse technology, supported by advances in Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, Mixed Reality and Extended Reality, offers new possibilities for immersive business education. However, existing research remains fragmented across individual technologies, educational contexts and learning outcomes, providing limited explanation of how the distinctive affordances of the Metaverse can be translated into theoretically grounded instructional design for business education. Through a structured review of the literature and theoretical analysis, this study examines how Metaverse‐based environments can support student engagement, practical skill development, business decision‐making and cross‐cultural collaboration. It integrates Constructivist Learning Theory, Experiential Learning Theory and Cognitive Load Theory to explain how learners construct knowledge through immersive participation, develop capabilities through experience and reflection, and avoid cognitive overload in complex virtual environments. The study also identifies major implementation challenges, including technological costs, hardware accessibility, privacy and security risks, educator readiness, and cross‐cultural adaptability. title: Chinese Doctoral Students' Boundary Crossing and Integration Into Communities of Practice in Hong Kong
text_snippet: Chinese Doctoral Students' Boundary Crossing and Integration Into Communities of Practice in Hong Kong ABSTRACT Research publications have emerged as the key marker of productivity determining one's survival in academia. The pressure to publish is no longer confined to faculty members but has extended to doctoral students. Despite a growing research interest in doctoral students' research writing experiences, there is a lack of scholarship investigating the complexities of the writing‐for‐publication process among those students who achieve publishing success during their studies. Informed by the dual concepts of boundary crossing and communities of practice and drawing on data from in‐depth interviews with four doctoral students and their supervisors, this study indicates that scholarly publishing is an intricate process encompassing the doctoral students' transition across linguistic, geographic, and emotional levels. This three‐tiered boundary crossing enabled the participants' socialization and integration into the academic research community. The paper concludes by providing valuable suggestions for doctoral students, supervisors, and university administrators.

title: Carving Out Professional Learning Paths and Challenges of Foreign Language Teacher Educators
text_snippet: Carving Out Professional Learning Paths and Challenges of Foreign Language Teacher Educators ABSTRACT Although professional learning (PL) practices of teacher educators have received some attention, the PL challenges of foreign language teacher educators in diverse contexts are under‐researched. Thus, this qualitative study aims to delineate the PL challenges regarding career aspirations, professional roles and research motivations of 22 senior professors in English Language Education programs in Türkiye, a country characterized by frequent reforms in education and teacher recruitment systems. We gathered the PL trajectories and challenges of the participants via semi‐structured interviews. The findings revealed that while the participants were mostly driven by internal motivations in their career aspirations and research motivations, a heavy lecturing workload, large class sizes, abrupt changes in promotion criteria, and a lack of financial and institutional support complicated their PL paths. The findings point to a compelling need for more institutional support and research facilities that can be actioned by universities to stabilize PL within a more massified system.

title: Predicting Grade 7 Academic Skills: The Role of Self‐Regulated Learning Competencies of Grade 2 Students
text_snippet: Predicting Grade 7 Academic Skills: The Role of Self‐Regulated Learning Competencies of Grade 2 Students ABSTRACT The article describes the model and standardized web‐based tool for assessing indicators of self‐regulated learning (SRL) from three areas—motivation, cognition, and metacognition. The aim of this exploratory study is to investigate which SRL indicators in Grade 2 predict students' academic skills in Grade 7. First, 401 Grade 2 students completed the SRL assessment. Of them, 321 students completed the Estonian language and 313 the math national test in Grade 7. All predictors were included simultaneously in the structural equation model. SRL indicators generally showed stronger associations with language than with math outcomes. Cognitive indicators, particularly attention, showed the most consistent predictive effects. The results are discussed in relation to students' developmental level and cognitive demands of different academic areas. Findings indicate that it is specifically important to support students' attention and thinking skills and create a classroom environment that fosters a growth mindset.

title: Instructional Design and Practice of an Interactive Animation Course for the Cultivation of Computational Thinking Ability With the Support of Flowcharts
text_snippet: Instructional Design and Practice of an Interactive Animation Course for the Cultivation of Computational Thinking Ability With the Support of Flowcharts ABSTRACT Computational thinking (CT) has received considerable attention as a key competency in education, yet effective approaches for developing CT remain limited. This quasi‐experimental study included 63 undergraduates to examine the effects of flowchart‐supported learning on CT. The experimental group received flowchart scaffolding and was split into high‐ and low‐scoring subgroups based on flowchart application scores, while the control group received conventional instruction. Results showed no significant between‐group differences in general CT after one semester, indicating that general CT is a relatively stable construct. Within the experimental group, however, students with high flowchart application scores exhibited significantly greater creativity and problem‐solving. Moreover, the experimental group performed significantly better on the individual comprehensive course project assessing practical CT. Findings suggest that although flowcharts did not improve self‐reported general CT in the short term, they significantly enhanced domain‐specific practical CT and, among proficient users, were associated with stronger domain‐specific cognitive CT abilities. This study provides empirical support for flowcharts as cognit

title: Unveiling the Fluid Impact of Self‐Concept and Self‐Efficacy Upon English Achievement: A Perspective of the Island Ridge Curve
text_snippet: Unveiling the Fluid Impact of Self‐Concept and Self‐Efficacy Upon English Achievement: A Perspective of the Island Ridge Curve ABSTRACT Self‐concept and self‐efficacy have received much attention from second/foreign language (L2) researchers. However, very few studies have empirically deciphered their similarities and distinctions. Even fewer have investigated how their contributions to L2 achievement vary across L2 proficiency levels. The current study examined the commonality and specificity of self‐concept and self‐efficacy and their relative contributions to English achievement and their fluid effects on English achievement across different proficiency groups based on the Island Ridge Curve theory. A sample of 369 Chinese undergraduate students completed two questionnaires of self‐concept and self‐efficacy, and their English achievement was represented using College English Test Band Six scores. Bifactor structural equation modeling (SEM) revealed that the combined scale shared one commonality factor and two specific factors. Multi‐group bifactor SEM found that the general factor and specific self‐concept factor were positively related to English achievement and their respective effects fluctuated across English proficiency groups.

title: Teacher–Student Relationship and School Bonding in Primary School as Longitudinal Predictors of Students' Academic Achievement
text_snippet: Teacher–Student Relationship and School Bonding in Primary School as Longitudinal Predictors of Students' Academic Achievement ABSTRACT This study adopts a multi‐informant (students and teachers) approach to explore the prospective associations of the teacher–student relationship and students' school bonding with students' academic achievement in primary school. The analytical sample consisted of 1349 Swiss children (Grade 1: 48.8% female; M age = 7.45, SD = 0.38, range 6.06–8.93) and 250 teachers. 976 children were followed up 5 years later (Grade 6; M age = 12.63, SD = 0.37, range 11.31–14.01). Sex, parental migration background, parental formal education level and the baseline of academic achievement at age 7 were control variables. Positive teacher–student relationship predicted mathematics achievement later. Positive teacher–student relationship and school bonding predicted language achievement later but not consistently. The quality of primary education teacher–student relationship seems to play a crucial role in students' academic achievement. Educational and political implications are discussed.

title: The Road Ahead: Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Experiential Learning in Higher Education
text_snippet: The Road Ahead: Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Experiential Learning in Higher Education ABSTRACT Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents promising opportunities to enhance experiential learning, but successful integration faces complex obstacles that require careful navigation. This systematic review followed the PRISMA guidelines to synthesise findings from 85 peer‐reviewed studies published in Scopus‐indexed journals on the application of AI technologies in experiential higher education across diverse domains. Results indicate that AI‐based tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, immersive simulations, and virtual reality environments can increase student engagement, motivation, self‐efficacy, and learning outcomes by providing interactive platforms aligned with experiential learning principles. However, findings also highlight significant challenges in effectively leveraging AI to complement rather than replace holistic, human‐centred educational experiences. Many current AI applications lack customisation for diverse learning styles and student backgrounds. Further research is critically needed on adaptive AI systems capable of providing personalised support tailored to individual learners' needs. Substantial teacher training and curriculum redesign are essential to capitalise fully on AI capabilities while delineating appropriate teacher versus technology roles

title: Exploring the Educational Linguistic Landscape Through Cultural Capital Theory: A Case Study of a Rural Primary School in China
text_snippet: Exploring the Educational Linguistic Landscape Through Cultural Capital Theory: A Case Study of a Rural Primary School in China ABSTRACT Research on linguistic landscapes in educational settings has highlighted their role in reflecting institutional ideologies and shaping school culture, yet little attention has been paid to rural schools, where signage may carry heightened symbolic significance. Grounded in Bourdieu's theory of cultural capital, this study aims to examine how cultural capital is represented and transmitted through a campus linguistic landscape of a rural primary school. Adopting a mixed‐methods design, the study collected data from a rural primary school, combining quantitative analysis of sign features with qualitative interpretation of students' perceptions. A total of 180 signs were collected, and interviews were conducted with 30 students to capture both visual patterns and lived experiences. Data were processed through content, discourse and thematic analyses. The findings reveal a predominantly monolingual and institutionally dominated landscape characterised by disciplinary and motivational functions. Five types of cultural capital emerged, namely institutionalised, educational, social normative, symbolic identity and participatory. Students demonstrated varied attitudes towards these messages, ranging from compliance to emotional resonance and aestheti

title: Examining the Role of Perceived Teacher Support on Left‐Behind Students' Well‐Being in China: The Mediation Role of Motivation and Resilience
text_snippet: Examining the Role of Perceived Teacher Support on Left‐Behind Students' Well‐Being in China: The Mediation Role of Motivation and Resilience ABSTRACT Since learners believe that their teachers can offer them chances to choose, support them in autonomous problem solving, and comprehend their internal feelings, teacher support results in the feeling of being loved and cared for. At the same time, the significance of motivation and resilience on the well‐being of left‐behind students (LBS) has been emphasized within the educational sphere. The present research investigated the way teacher support affects learners' well‐being, with internal motivation and educational resilience as mediators. A total of 258 LBS were surveyed in the present research. The results revealed that teacher support significantly predicted both resilience and motivation (explaining 26.4% and 46.6% of their variance, respectively). Both mediators, in turn, significantly predicted well‐being. The model explained 18.7% of the variance in well‐being. The study indicated the significance of teacher support to the LBS's well‐being; therefore, maintaining the theoretical importance for enhancing their motivation and resilience.

title: School Leadership Perspectives on Policies Related to Open Educational Resources in Primary and Secondary Education: Implications for Policy Development Through the Lens of UNESCO 's Recommendations
text_snippet: School Leadership Perspectives on Policies Related to Open Educational Resources in Primary and Secondary Education: Implications for Policy Development Through the Lens of UNESCO 's Recommendations ABSTRACT To ensure inclusive and equitable quality education for all, high‐quality open educational resources (OER) are essential. However, the lack of appropriate policies governing the development and adoption of OER presents a barrier to their application in schools. Based on relevant UNESCO guidelines of OER, this study aims to inform policy development by leveraging insights from school leaders in Hong Kong. A territory‐wide survey of 102 school leaders, representing over 10% of Hong Kong schools, and follow‐up interviews with approximately 20% of the survey participants who volunteered to be interviewed ( n = 19) were conducted to investigate current school policies related to OER. Situated within schools' broader digital‐resource practices, the findings reveal areas requiring government intervention to address challenges, including resource accessibility, quality assurance, the need for teacher training, and the establishment of clear guidelines for resource adoption. In line with UNESCO's Building Blocks for OER policy development, this study provides insights into policy interventions that encompass (1) resource development and management strategies at both territorial and

title: The Role of Faith‐Based Organisations in ‘Secular’ International Development Education: Theorising Religions and Development With an Exploratory Case Study
text_snippet: The Role of Faith‐Based Organisations in ‘Secular’ International Development Education: Theorising Religions and Development With an Exploratory Case Study ABSTRACT Faith‐based organisations (FBOs) are recognised by the development community as key organisations and partners in development cooperation. Yet commitments to secularism underlying international development cooperation in policy and practice have—to a certain extent—restricted theoretical and empirical study of the involvement and contribution of FBOs in development cooperation in general and development education in particular. With this paper, we aim to widen our conceptual approach to the role of religion in international development education by engaging a theory of non‐Western secularism. With this theoretical development, we analyse an exploratory case study of the Presentation congregation and its global advocacy mission, the International Presentation Association, as a space to consider the role of FBOs in international development education through the lens of non‐Western secularism.

title: The Effect of Nursing Students' Metaverse Perception on Flexible Thinking in Learning: A Path Analysis
text_snippet: The Effect of Nursing Students' Metaverse Perception on Flexible Thinking in Learning: A Path Analysis ABSTRACT It is expected that nursing students will demonstrate flexibility in their thinking as they learn, enabling them to solve problems, produce solutions, and establish cooperation. The development of flexible thinking can be facilitated by the use of the metaverse, which is a technological innovation and a three‐dimensional virtual world. This study aims to examine how nursing students' metaverse perception affects flexible thinking in learning and to investigate the relationship between them. This research has a descriptive and exploratory design. The study was conducted between October and November 2024 with the participation of 494 nursing students. Three instruments were employed for the collection of data in a face‐to‐face setting within the classroom environment. The instruments utilized in the study were the Descriptive Characteristics Form, the Metaverse Perception Scale for Nursing Students, and the Flexible Thinking in Learning Scale. The statistical analysis was conducted with a significance value of p β = 0.653, R = 0.590, p

title: School Climate, Teaching Enjoyment, Resilience and Work Engagement Among University Teachers in AI ‐Driven Higher Education: A Multi‐Group Structural Equation Modelling Study
text_snippet: School Climate, Teaching Enjoyment, Resilience and Work Engagement Among University Teachers in AI ‐Driven Higher Education: A Multi‐Group Structural Equation Modelling Study ABSTRACT This study investigated the relationships among school climate, teaching enjoyment, resilience and work engagement among university teachers, while further examining gender differences in these relationships. An explanatory sequential mixed‐methods design was adopted. In the quantitative phase, survey data were collected from 658 university teachers and analysed using structural equation modelling and multi‐group analysis. The quantitative data were processed using SPSS 27.0 and AMOS 26.0, while the qualitative interview data were analysed with MAXQDA 24 through thematic analysis. In the qualitative phase, semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 10 teachers to further explain the observed gender differences. The results showed that school climate was positively associated with teaching enjoyment, resilience and work engagement, while both teaching enjoyment and resilience were positively associated with work engagement. In addition, significant gender differences were found in two structural paths: the association between school climate and work engagement was stronger among male teachers, whereas the association between teaching enjoyment and work engagement was stronger among female teach

title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Dual Perspective From Academics and Students on Its Transformative Potential
text_snippet: Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Dual Perspective From Academics and Students on Its Transformative Potential ABSTRACT This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in higher education institutions in Kazakhstan. It aims to explore students' and academics' perceptions, usage patterns, challenges, and training needs. The findings show that AI is increasingly seen as a transformative academic tool, especially for research, language learning, writing support and problem‐solving. Although many participants first encountered AI through media exposure or academic requirements, their engagement has shifted from initial scepticism to routine use, with many reporting daily reliance on AI tools. Participants highlighted AI's potential to create more personalised and interactive learning environments, particularly through applications like chatbots and adaptive learning systems. However, concerns were raised about over‐dependence on AI, which could weaken critical thinking and problem‐solving skills. These concerns align with previous research warning of passive learning behaviours in AI‐supported educational settings. Despite widespread AI adoption, the study identifies significant gaps in institutional infrastructure and the absence of systematic training programmes. Most participants developed their AI skills through informal, self‐guided l

title: The Interplay of Positive Reframing, Mindfulness, and Growth Mindset in Shaping Career Aspirations: A Mixed‐Methods Study
text_snippet: The Interplay of Positive Reframing, Mindfulness, and Growth Mindset in Shaping Career Aspirations: A Mixed‐Methods Study ABSTRACT This study investigates the associations among positive reframing, mindfulness, growth mindset, and career aspirations in a sample of 308 undergraduate students from a public university in Eastern China. Using a convergent parallel mixed‐methods design, quantitative data were collected through validated self‐report scales, and qualitative data were gathered via semi‐structured interviews with a subset of 20 participants. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) revealed significant direct and indirect pathways of positive reframing and mindfulness in relation to career aspirations, with growth mindset as a significant mediator in these relationships. The thematic analysis of the interview data provided deeper insights, illustrating how students leverage positive reframing and mindfulness to cultivate resilience, focus, and self‐awareness, which in turn are linked to a growth mindset and ambitious career goals. The integration of quantitative and qualitative findings underscores the pivotal role of a growth mindset as a foundation for career development and highlights the need for interventions that foster positive psychological traits in students. This study contributes to the understanding of how cognitive and affective factors interact and are associat

title: “Histogogy”: Trend and Thematic Analysis on Pedagogical History Education (1993–2024)
text_snippet: “Histogogy”: Trend and Thematic Analysis on Pedagogical History Education (1993–2024) ABSTRACT In history education, pedagogy is essential, particularly for fostering students' understanding of history. The ongoing dearth of thorough and insightful research on research trends and hotspots demonstrates the goal of this study. This study focuses on a bibliometric examination of patterns in pedagogical history teaching goals. Using the WoS database, 600 research publications spanning 1993 to 2024 were examined. The data was exported to VOSviewer, Bibliometrix, and Microsoft Excel. The findings demonstrated that teacher preparation is the primary area of interest in research on virtual tours for learning, with significant publication activity in the United States, Brazil, and Spain. The “Journal of Curriculum Studies” was the most excellent and convincing source, and the University of Murcia was the pioneering organization. The four domains were identified using the thematic map, and new regions were found. The study's findings may help foster global collaboration, strengthen the link between history and education, improve educational design, and identify new areas of study for academics, instructors, and educational policymakers.

title: Beyond Administration: How School Governance Practices Foster Happiness and Belonging Among Primary Students
text_snippet: Beyond Administration: How School Governance Practices Foster Happiness and Belonging Among Primary Students ABSTRACT Schools are not only instructional settings but also critical social environments in which students' emotional well‐being, sense of belonging, and agency are shaped. While previous research has emphasized the role of student voice in democratic schooling, limited empirical evidence exists on how governance‐oriented practices function in primary education through participatory interventions. This study investigates how governance‐based practices influence primary students' school happiness and sense of belonging through an action research approach. Conducted in a public primary school in Türkiye, the study involved 15 third‐ and fourth‐grade students and employed semi‐structured interviews before and after the implementation of participatory governance practices. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis. The findings reveal that structured opportunities for representation and shared decision‐making enhance students' emotional well‐being, strengthen their sense of belonging, and foster greater engagement with school life. Students who perceived their voices as valued reported increased confidence, motivation, and psychological security, whereas limited participation and authoritarian practices were associated with feelings of marginalization and reduc

title: Transformations in Children's Play in Rural Areas: Teachers' and Parents' Perspectives
text_snippet: Transformations in Children's Play in Rural Areas: Teachers' and Parents' Perspectives ABSTRACT Play for young children in rural areas is changing with social, cultural shifts and increased digitaltechnology use. This study explores changes in play among children aged 4–6 in three Gunungkidul villages, from parents' and ECE teachers' perspectives. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, data from 21 parents and six teachers were collected via online questionnaires and analysed thematically. The findings indicate that children's play has evolved into a hybrid play ecology in which physical, social, imaginative, traditional and digital play coexist across homes, schools and communities, rather than shifting linearly towards digital play. However, notable changes were observed in the context and proportion of play, including increased indoor and individual play, reduced spontaneous group play, a weakening of traditional play transmission and shorter durations of imaginative engagement. These shifts were associated with digital access, weakened peer ecosystems, parental safety concerns, changing family time structures, the use of devices as time‐filling and calming tools and post‐pandemic social habits. The study highlights the need for school–family collaboration and context‐sensitive digital parenting and media mediation strategies to support balanced and developmentally meanin

title: Goals of Well‐Being in the Context of Finnish Comprehensive School Education
text_snippet: Goals of Well‐Being in the Context of Finnish Comprehensive School Education ABSTRACT One of the central aims of education and educational policies is to promote well‐being. Laws and norms oblige Finnish schools to formulate the goals for improving the well‐being of the entire school community in the documents guiding the school's operations. However, little is known about how the policy shows up in the school‐level goals related to well‐being, and how the ambiguous concept of well‐being has been understood. This article examines the well‐being discourses that emerged in the documents guiding the operations of Finnish comprehensive schools. We collected 379 school‐level documents from 20 municipalities and analysed the data using discourse analysis. As a result, four discourses were identified: the individual‐centred, competence‐related, collaboration‐related, and development‐supporting discourses. Our results indicated that well‐being at school is not an unambiguous or universal goal. Goals related to well‐being are often described at an abstract level. The trends in education policy affect the discourses that emerge and produce goals in the plans that partly follow the paradigms related to schools and society.

title: Before and After Remedial Classes: Students' Attitudes, Perceived Learning and Behavioural Intentions in Higher Education Accounting
text_snippet: Before and After Remedial Classes: Students' Attitudes, Perceived Learning and Behavioural Intentions in Higher Education Accounting ABSTRACT This study examines the role of remedial classes as a pedagogical intervention in higher education accounting. Specifically, it analyses how students' attitudes, perceived learning, continued‐use intention and word‐of‐mouth communication are shaped before and after participation in remedial classes. A quantitative pre‐ and post‐intervention design was adopted, with data collected from accounting students at two moments: before the implementation of the remedial classes and after their completion. The study used previously validated scales to measure reciprocal benefits, social influence, recognition, motivation, attitude, continued‐use intention, word‐of‐mouth and perceived learning. Structural equation modelling was used to test the relationships among the constructs at both time points. The descriptive results showed that students' evaluations became more moderate after the intervention, suggesting a shift from expectation‐based perceptions to experience‐based evaluations. The structural results revealed that reciprocal benefits, social influence, and recognition positively influenced students' attitudes both before and after the remedial classes. However, reciprocal benefits and social influence became stronger predictors of attitude a

title: Exploring Teachers' Professional Identity Profiles in China: A Latent Profile Analysis
text_snippet: Exploring Teachers' Professional Identity Profiles in China: A Latent Profile Analysis ABSTRACT This study examined the heterogeneity of professional identity among Chinese teachers and estimated the predictive effects of demographic and psychological factors on professional identity profiles based on the self‐determination theory (SDT). Data were collected from 404 teachers in mainland China and analysed using unconditional and conditional latent profile analyses. Three professional identity profiles were identified: engaged teachers, involved teachers and dedicated teachers. The results showed that two demographic covariates (i.e., teaching level of elementary school, teaching experience of 9 years or less) significantly predicted profile membership. Additionally, significant differences were observed among the profiles in terms of teachers' basic psychological needs of competence and relatedness, in line with SDT. This research contributed to a more comprehensive understanding of the mechanism underlying teacher professional identity development and guided effective practices in teacher education.

title: Meaningful Physical Education in Focus. A Scoping Review
text_snippet: Meaningful Physical Education in Focus. A Scoping Review ABSTRACT Meaningful Physical Education (MPE) is a student‐centred approach aimed at fostering sustained participation in active lifestyles, yet evidence is fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map existing MPE research in formal educational contexts and to identify methodological, contextual and pedagogical patterns informing future research and practice. Following a five‐stage methodological framework and PRISMA‐ScR, we searched ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar for English/Spanish studies (2017–2025) explicitly referencing MPE in formal education. Of 237 records, 44 met inclusion criteria. Studies were concentrated in Canada and Ireland, with emerging contributions from Spain and other countries, and focused mainly on primary/secondary schooling and physical education teacher education. Qualitative self‐studies and case studies predominated, while quantitative and mixed‐methods designs are increasing. Reported benefits included higher student motivation, engagement, and enjoyment and enhanced teacher reflection; constraints included limited time, institutional support and curricular tensions. We propose an integrative account organized around three intersecting trajectories: methodological, contextual and pedagogical, framed by adherence to PA as the unifying horizon and the emergence of MPE as a poten

title: Understanding Student Engagement in AI ‐Assisted Learning in Higher Education: The Roles of AI Support, Teacher Support and Flow
text_snippet: Understanding Student Engagement in AI ‐Assisted Learning in Higher Education: The Roles of AI Support, Teacher Support and Flow ABSTRACT With the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, this study examined how AI support, teacher support and flow are associated with student engagement in AI‐assisted learning in higher education. Drawing on Self‐Determination Theory, a cross‐sectional survey was conducted with 677 university students from multiple institutions who had prior experience using AI‐enabled tools for learning. Data were analysed using structural equation modelling with AMOS 26.0 to examine the hypothesised relationships among the study variables. The results showed that AI support and teacher support were both positively associated with student engagement. In addition, both forms of support were positively associated with flow and flow was positively associated with engagement. Mediation analyses further indicated that flow mediated the associations between AI support and engagement and between teacher support and engagement. These findings suggest that student engagement in AI‐assisted learning is linked not only to the availability of technological and interpersonal support, but also to the extent to which students experience learning as focused, absorbing and meaningful. title: Teacher Educators as Sustainability Change Agents: Identity, Agency, and Disciplinary Cultures in EFL and Social Sciences Programmes
text_snippet: Teacher Educators as Sustainability Change Agents: Identity, Agency, and Disciplinary Cultures in EFL and Social Sciences Programmes ABSTRACT Sustainability education (SE) is increasingly recognized as a critical aspect of higher education and teacher education due to global environmental, social, and economic challenges. However, limited research has examined how teacher educators in developing countries, including Iran, conceptualize and implement sustainability in their teaching practices. This qualitative narrative study explored how Iranian English as a Foreign Language (EFL) and Social Science (SS) teacher educators interpret and enact sustainability through the Identity–Agency–Disciplinary (IAD) framework. Twenty semi‐structured interviews were conducted with teacher educators from four public universities in Iran, and thematic analysis was performed using NVivo software. Findings indicate a complex, recursive relationship between sustainability literacy and sustainability implementation. EFL teacher educators exhibited strong awareness of sustainable practices' outcomes but reported limited integration of sustainability into their professional identity, enacting only partial sustainable practices. Conversely, SS teacher educators demonstrated conceptual understanding of sustainability but experienced identity fragmentation and resistance to practical implementation. Acr

title: Moment‐to‐Moment Dynamics of Foreign Language Enjoyment: An Idiodynamic Study of Conversational Topics Among Young Language Learners
text_snippet: Moment‐to‐Moment Dynamics of Foreign Language Enjoyment: An Idiodynamic Study of Conversational Topics Among Young Language Learners ABSTRACT Foreign Language Enjoyment has received increasing attention in second language acquisition due to its role in fostering engagement and communication. Although previous research has often treated enjoyment as a relatively stable trait, perspectives informed by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST) suggest that emotions are dynamic, non‐ergodic, and fluctuate over time. Drawing on CDST, the present study adopts an idiographic approach to investigate second‐by‐second changes in foreign language enjoyment during conversational tasks. Six young language learners participated in recorded interactions on four different conversational topics, followed by idiodynamic self‐ratings and stimulated recall interviews to explain emotional fluctuations. The findings revealed nonlinear, individualized trajectories of enjoyment, highlighting substantial within‐person variability. Fluctuations were closely linked to topic familiarity and interest, idea availability, perceived task difficulty, and cognitive effort. Familiar and meaningful topics generally facilitated higher enjoyment, whereas unfamiliar or cognitively demanding topics led to declines; however, moderate challenge occasionally enhanced engagement.
