title: Beyond dichotomies: unravelling the complexities of international standardised English language testing
text_snippet: Beyond dichotomies: unravelling the complexities of international standardised English language testing Abstract This article discusses the issues raised in O’Sullivan’s and Hashimura et al.’s Point-Counterpoint articles with the aim of introducing new angles on the topic of international standardised English language testing and opening the debate further. In the first section, I provide summaries of the positions taken by O’Sullivan and Hashimura et al., contrasting the “tests as a social good” and “critical language testing” paradigms. Second, I explore international standardised English language testing as a site of complexity, focusing on the nature of this complexity in conceptualising language testing as a field, language tests (as social objects), and language testing organisations. Third, I address shifts towards measuring innovative constructs and the prospect of greater localisation. Finally, I conclude with a call for research that explores complexity in greater depth with a view to change.

title: Pedagogically grounded AI use in the EFL classroom: principles and classroom examples
text_snippet: Pedagogically grounded AI use in the EFL classroom: principles and classroom examples Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is now widely available to teachers and learners through natural language prompts. While such tools create new opportunities for English language teaching, their classroom use often remains exploratory and detached from pedagogical aims. This article argues for a pedagogy-first approach, where AI use is deliberately aligned with learning objectives. Drawing on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and its recent adaptation to AI (AI-TPACK), the article shows how teachers can integrate technological, content, and pedagogical knowledge to ensure AI supports, rather than drives, language learning. The discussion is illustrated with adaptable and practical classroom examples that build AI literacy, enhance student engagement, and encourage critical reflection on the ethical and pedagogical boundaries of AI.

title: Principles of GenAI-assisted microlearning: perspectives of pre-service language teachers
text_snippet: Principles of GenAI-assisted microlearning: perspectives of pre-service language teachers Abstract This qualitative research explored pre-service language teachers’ perceptions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted microlearning in an ELT technology integration class. In semi-structured interviews, 14 Hong Kong pre-service teachers reflected on their engagement with adaptive, multimodal microlearning activities designed to minimize cognitive load. They valued GenAI’s personalized, real-time adaptability, interactivity, and instant feedback. However, they expressed concerns regarding learner autonomy, over-reliance on AI scaffolding, and content accuracy and transparency. They emphasized the critical role of human teachers in mediating and contextualizing GenAI use. Four pedagogical principles for effective AI-supported microlearning were identified: real-time adaptability, multimodal interactivity, learner customization, and reliability and accuracy. These principles reflect the unique affordances of the microlearning format—namely, that it is short, focused, and repeatable—rather than general GenAI features. This study provides suggestions for educators and content creators wishing to integrate GenAI thoughtfully into microlearning-based ELT.

title: International tests can benefit teachers and learners
text_snippet: International tests can benefit teachers and learners Abstract In this paper, I present a set of arguments in support of the proposition that international standardized tests (IST) are beneficial to teachers and learners. The arguments are designed to defend the proposition from the IATEFL debate and not to offer a balanced discussion and are based on my experience as a teacher, researcher, and test developer, with some support offered from the published literature. Before presenting my arguments, I take time to briefly reflect on the drivers and objectives that lay behind the origins of standardized testing. I then consider the benefits of ISTs to learners and teachers before reflecting on the obligations of developers to teachers and learners. Without a recognition of these obligations, ISTs can never meet the needs of language learning systems.

title: Supporting student-led interactions in virtual exchange
text_snippet: Supporting student-led interactions in virtual exchange Abstract Virtual exchange (VE) is becoming integral to many university curricula, yet students navigate VE with varying degrees of success. Despite extensive research, the role of oral interaction skills remains underexplored, especially in VE, where interactional conditions diverge from those in the classroom. This study applies conversation analysis to a fifteen-hour corpus of video-recorded meetings with students from Germany, Israel, and Spain, collaborating in online intercultural groups of three or four in an English-as-a-lingua-franca setting. Focusing on three features of the student-led interactions, namely task management, translanguaging, and cultural incidents, our findings show that conversation flow is enhanced when task management is collaborative, inclusive, and explicit, translanguaging is used strategically without excluding others, and cultural incidents are addressed constructively. These findings have important pedagogic implications for developing interactional and intercultural competence and provide essential preparation for both online and face-to-face language learners.

title: No-code approaches to developing ELT resources with generative artificial intelligence
text_snippet: No-code approaches to developing ELT resources with generative artificial intelligence Abstract In this series, we explore technology-related themes and topics. The series aims to discuss and demystify what may be new areas for some readers and to consider their relevance for English language teachers. Advances in the no-code approach that uses generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have enabled practitioners to develop ELT resources and tools without having programming expertise. More recently, within the ELT field, vibe coding has emerged. This approach allows instructors to develop and revise customized apps by interacting with GenAI and by using natural language alone. These innovations hold significant promise for ELT because teachers can now create resources such as chatbots for language practice, automated essay-scoring tools, and language exercise apps tailored to their needs, without relying on IT professionals. This feature article introduces three currently available approaches to developing a GenAI-mediated tool and discusses their merits and challenges in the ELT domain.

title: Genre pedagogy to teach spoken reports in EFL
text_snippet: Genre pedagogy to teach spoken reports in EFL Abstract Genre-based pedagogy is an approach for promoting school literacy that uses texts as basis for instruction. Since its origins in the 1980s, however, this pedagogy has emphasized written literacy, paying less attention to students’ spoken communication, particularly in EFL classrooms. To address this gap, this study assesses whether genre-based pedagogy may also promote students’ spoken communication. We adapted this pedagogy to help sixth graders create spoken descriptive reports in an EFL Colombian classroom. Our adaptation, called talking to learn (T2L), consists of a scaffolded instructional cycle that uses authentic spoken texts as the starting point for instruction. Using a case study-mixed methods design, we collected data from pre– and post–test spoken tasks, observations, and interviews. Quantitative and qualitative analyses were integrated with a joint display. Findings suggest that T2L helped students produce well-organized spoken descriptive reports, becoming a valuable tool for developing students’ ability to create meaning in EFL.

title: Moroccan EFL teachers’ experiences with the 2023 Al-Haouz earthquake
text_snippet: Moroccan EFL teachers’ experiences with the 2023 Al-Haouz earthquake Abstract This quantitative study examines Moroccan English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers’ experiences following the 2023 Al-Haouz earthquake, the country’s most devastating natural disaster in six decades. Using an online survey (n = 133) grounded in social-emotional learning (SEL), trauma-sensitive pedagogy, and resilience frameworks, the study explored teachers’ experiences in relation to challenges, growth, coping mechanisms, and preparedness levels. Descriptive analyses revealed significant emotional and professional strain, including material loss, disrupted instruction, and limited institutional support. Yet, most teachers reported sustained commitment to teaching and strong reliance on personal and relational coping resources such as faith, community support, and helping others. Findings highlight teachers’ dual roles as educators and emotional caregivers and underscore the urgency of integrating trauma-sensitive practices and SEL principles into national teacher preparation and crisis recovery plans. The study contributes to growing discussions on teacher well-being, autonomy, and resilience in disaster-affected educational contexts.

title: Fairness for sale: the hidden costs of international language tests
text_snippet: Fairness for sale: the hidden costs of international language tests Abstract This Counterpoint challenges the claim that international standardised assessments benefit both learners and teachers. While acknowledging that such tests are unlikely to disappear, we argue that they harm language education. We first deconstruct the historical myths used to legitimise standardisation, revealing it as a rhetorical move that substitutes genealogy for evidence. We then trace the resulting harms in three ways: mechanistically, through overstandardisation that flattens language and threatens validity; systemically, through the economic machinery of the testing-industrial complex, where ‘edu-washing’ casts profit as benevolence; and ideologically, through a fiction of fairness that conflates sameness with justice, concealing raciolinguistic, and algorithmic biases. Against this, we propose a human-centred re-orientation of assessment, where validity is both statistical and ethical, and fairness an ongoing relationship rather than a calculation. Reform, we suggest, will not come from better metrics but from empathy, from a willingness to remember what it feels like to be measured.

title: Beyond detection: GenAI in EAL writing education
text_snippet: Beyond detection: GenAI in EAL writing education Abstract This study investigates how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) shapes the writing practices of five Chinese English as an additional language (EAL) students and how emerging GenAI-text detection practices mediate that use. Findings from screen-recordings, written drafts, and interviews reveal four recurrent functions of GenAI use, that is, brainstorming, structuring, occasional drafting, and revising, yet students calibrated their reliance on each function against the perceived risk of being flagged by GenAI detectors. To mitigate that risk, participants shuttled between ChatGPT, Grammarly, and self-paraphrase to ‘humanise’ GenAI output, occasionally reallocating effort from idea development to surface revision. The study, therefore, problematises a detection-first approach, showing that it (1) engenders strategic but pedagogically hollow text manipulation, (2) complicates ‘plagiarised’ versus ‘original’ writing, and (3) potentially shifts assessment towards product-centric criteria. The study argues for cultivating critical AI literacy so that GenAI-assisted EAL writing instruction can prioritize creativity, voice, and argument quality over algorithmic policing.

title: Reimagining ELT: nomadic knowledging and nomadic languaging
text_snippet: Reimagining ELT: nomadic knowledging and nomadic languaging Abstract Drawing on an ethnographic study with the Mongolian nomadic herders - xууч xөөрөх - loosely translated as “nomadic reminiscing circle,” this article seeks to expand the growing decolonial languaging turn in ELT. It introduces the intertwined land-based cosmologies of “nomadic knowledging” and “nomadic languaging,” drawing on a philosophy where life, nature, time, language, and identity are understood as inherently fluid but attuned to the cycles of the land. Yet, this fluidity exists in tension with the contextual rootedness - the need for linguistic boundaries to protect nomadic knowledge systems. English is welcomed into the Mongolian nomadic cosmologies only when it enters with humility, respect and care. This tension highlights that the languaging turn in ELT must attend not only to fluidity but also to rootedness. Just as nomads adapt to ever-changing environments, ELT must remain responsive to shifting identities, evolving language practices and contextualized local practices.

title: Pragmatics in Japanese EFL education: textbook and teacher insights
text_snippet: Pragmatics in Japanese EFL education: textbook and teacher insights Abstract This study examined how the most recent government-approved English textbooks and high school English teachers in Japan address pragmatics in the context of speech acts. A page-by-page analysis of twelve textbooks coded explicitly presented general pragmatic information, along with the types and presentation formats of speech acts. Teachers’ awareness and instruction of pragmatic content were explored through an online survey of forty-six in-service high school teachers and follow-up interviews with a subset of five participants. The textbook analysis revealed limited coverage of pragmatics and little information on the contextual use of speech acts. The teacher survey suggested that although many teachers had limited knowledge of pragmatics, they compensated for textbook limitations in improvised ways rather than through systematic planning. The study concludes that while textbook designers and teachers should address pragmatics in a consistent and sufficient manner, the absence of a standardized curriculum of pragmatics may hinder this goal.

title: Using ChatGPT as a “Friend” in reflective critical friendships
text_snippet: Using ChatGPT as a “Friend” in reflective critical friendships Abstract Reflective practice has long been regarded as a cornerstone of language teacher education and development, typically enacted through dialogue with trusted colleagues or critical friendships (CFs). Such human-to-human exchanges are grounded in trust, contextual understanding, and professional experience, and they play a central role in shaping teachers’ professional development. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, however, invites new possibilities for reflection by offering teachers instant access to dialogue that is probing, structured, and nonjudgmental. This study examines the potential of ChatGPT to act as a form of CF in reflective practice, comparing its contributions with those of human interlocutors. We consider benefits such as immediacy, breadth of perspectives, and creative provocation, alongside significant limitations, including the absence of trust, lived experience, and relational aspects. Ethical concerns, particularly those relating to bias, cultural representation, privacy, and the risk of over-reliance, are also foregrounded. We argue that while ChatGPT may usefully supplement reflective practice, especially for teachers with limited access to professional networks, it cannot replace the dialogic, situated, and relational qualities of human CF.

title: Facilitating professional growth through materials-based assessments
text_snippet: Facilitating professional growth through materials-based assessments Abstract The burgeoning scholarship about teaching materials has been reflected in a growing number of teacher education courses including instruction in materials development. However, we know little about how student–teachers in teacher education courses develop a knowledge base about materials which they can use in their practice as English language teacher. Addressing the dearth of publications in materials development in teacher education, here we report findings from a study that explored the impact of a professional development qualification for in-service teachers that uses materials evaluation, adaptation, and creation as the core components of assessment. Data from multiple interviews with three teacher participants shows that the articulation of materials evaluation, adaptation, and design in the assessed tasks granted them concrete opportunities to develop in the areas of materials adaptation and design. This allows teachers to meet learners’ needs as well as developing their professional confidence.

title: Trauma-sensitive English teaching and SEL amid war in Ukraine
text_snippet: Trauma-sensitive English teaching and SEL amid war in Ukraine Abstract The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine unleashed a collective trauma that has impacted all within the country, including educators attempting to support their students. This action research explored how an English teacher in Ukraine implemented and evaluated classroom activities founded upon trauma-sensitive teaching, social-emotional learning, and resilience-building. Participants completed individual activity surveys and a final survey. In response to the research question: How do students living and learning in a wartime crisis perceive teaching strategies based in trauma-sensitive teaching, social-emotional learning, and resilience building in the English classroom?, descriptive statistics determined that students rated all activities positively. Qualitative analysis of participant comments found that students: described the activities as engaging and distracting them from their worries; valued the discussions for both connection-building and language development; felt the limits of their English proficiency; and demonstrated the complex responses of those living through ongoing war-related trauma.

title: Children’s learning through digital technologies: an introduction
text_snippet: Children’s learning through digital technologies: an introduction Abstract This introductory article sets the scene for this Special Issue on ‘Children’s Learning Through Digital Technologies’. We begin by outlining key issues in this area: the valuable opportunities such technologies offer children to develop English language and other skills; their limited use in primary English classrooms; the relative scarcity of research into 6- to 14-year-olds’ digital activity which generally focuses on just a few research settings. We then introduce the seven Special Issue contributions that explore children’s digital experiences at home and school, teachers’ perceptions, classroom practices, and teaching strategies. The articles also showcase age-appropriate methods for working with children. Finally, we consider some broader implications and challenges of integrating digital technologies into children’s learning. Our aim is for this Special Issue to encourage practitioners and researchers to consider how digital technologies can be used and studied in their own young learner contexts.

title: Primary EFL teachers’ perceptions of technology to support speaking
text_snippet: Primary EFL teachers’ perceptions of technology to support speaking Abstract This study examines the perceptions of pre-service and in-service teachers on the use of technology-enhanced tasks to support children in speaking English in diverse primary EFL classrooms. Research on both primary EFL teachers’ perceptions and technology-enhanced speaking tasks for young learners is scant. This study addresses these gaps by exploring the views of participating pre-service and in-service EFL teachers. To gather data, three technology-enhanced projects were implemented in primary EFL classrooms and participant interviews conducted. Prior to data collection, a workshop was held to train participants in using technology. Interview findings suggest that participants considered various aspects of gamification, such as sequencing tasks, competition, and collaboration, to be crucial when designing and implementing technology-enhanced tasks to support young foreign language learners in speaking English. The results also highlight teachers’ desire for greater support, including teacher training, to enable them to implement such tasks.

title: Challenges in understanding children’s language learning in games
text_snippet: Challenges in understanding children’s language learning in games Abstract This article explores the challenges teachers and researchers face in understanding children’s English learning outside formal contexts, with a focus on digital game playing. The discussion is based on the author’s experience and self-reflection during participation in the cross-national project ‘Language Learning in the Wild’. However, it is believed that many of the challenges addressed here are not unique to this particular project. Therefore, sharing them may benefit researchers and educators interested in understanding the relationship between young learners’ game-playing and their English learning. The article highlights challenges such as establishing a shared understanding of ‘digital games’ among stakeholders in a given context; adopting methodologies that are theoretically sound and ethically appropriate; and reconceptualizing and operationalizing learning outcomes that are better suited to an increasingly digitalized learning environment and lifestyle. The article concludes with implications for understanding and utilizing digital games in both research and practice.

title: Digital game-based language learning in the young L2 learner classroom
text_snippet: Digital game-based language learning in the young L2 learner classroom Abstract Digital game-based language learning (DGBLL) aims to enhance L2 learners’ language and literacy skills through the purposeful integration of digital games not designed for language practice. This approach can provide opportunities for learners to be exposed to and use L2 in authentic, meaningful contexts, with a focus on both meaning and form. It can also promote collaboration, creative problem solving, and critical thinking, and is associated with situated learning, intrinsic motivation, and clear objectives and assessment. This article sets out some practical considerations to guide practitioners in planning for and designing DGBLL. It then analyses three DGBLL exemplars, designed and implemented by the author in young L2 learner classrooms in Spain and Hong Kong. Each exemplar is evaluated using a framework based on the principles of task-based language teaching and ideas drawn from the broader literature on game-based learning.

title: Enjoyment, engagement, and success in children’s digital EFL games
text_snippet: Enjoyment, engagement, and success in children’s digital EFL games Abstract Game-based language learning can be enjoyable and effective for young learners, but it is not clear that enjoyment precipitates effectiveness. We investigated the relationships between engagement and success in game-based language learning for young language learners. This study reports data from 125 Spanish/Catalan 11- to 12-year-old students playing EFL literacy minigames. Learners answered a questionnaire about engagement with English classes and with the minigames, and gameplay data were collected from the game logs. We show that increased minigame use was due to successful language use during gameplay or positive attitudes towards the use of game-based language learning, but not both for the same students. Clustering students based on engagement revealed that an otherwise-unengaged group became engaged with language content through game use. We encourage the use of game-based language learning for children as one activity among many, including the use of supplementary materials to help learners understand that games can be effective language-learning tools.

title: Exploring six-year-olds’ L2 English digital learning in the home
text_snippet: Exploring six-year-olds’ L2 English digital learning in the home Abstract Young L2 English learners constitute an underresearched group in the fields of L2 acquisition and ELT. However, emerging research has shown that young children learn English informally, even prior to formal instruction in school, often influenced by their engagement in English-language media, such as watching YouTube and gaming. This study adopts an ethnographic perspective to explore how three six-year-olds in Norway engage with English-language media platforms and games in their homes, and how such engagement influences L2 learning. The study’s focus is on methodological and ethical issues when researching children in private spheres. Data were collected through a show-and-tell procedure which demanded thorough ethnographic groundwork and considerable researcher flexibility. The findings showed that all three homes offered affordances for L2 learning. We argue that in order to capture socially situated engagement with digital technologies, it was crucial to collect data in the actual socially situated practice in the young learners’ homes.

title: ‘Did a robot write that?’: AI-generated digital storybooks
text_snippet: ‘Did a robot write that?’: AI-generated digital storybooks Abstract ‘Did a robot write that?’ asked one young participant in this study. A deceptively simple question that captures the challenges raised by artificial intelligence (AI) in children’s literacy experiences. This article explores how young children and their caregivers engage with AI-generated storybooks through Let’s Story, a feature of the Applaydu app. Developed by Gameloft and Ferrero International in partnership with the University of Oxford’s Learning in Families through Technology project, Let’s Story enables families to co-create storybooks using Microsoft’s generative AI tools. Data were collected through two play tests involving 22 parent–child pairs from the United Kingdom, United States, and France. These sessions examined how the children and their caregivers responded to AI-generated content during shared reading. While the stories supported playful engagement, especially in a child’s home language, concerns emerged about narrative complexity, image-text alignment, and narration. The findings offer timely insights for ELT practitioners and educational technology developers.

title: Children and gaming: how do they help themselves learn English?
text_snippet: Children and gaming: how do they help themselves learn English? Abstract This study explores the video gaming habits of twenty-eight avid gamers aged 9–14 years old who played in English from Chile, China, Hungary, and India. Using participatory interviews, we examined the language learning strategies these child gamers used to navigate the challenges of playing in English. Findings revealed that the children were highly motivated to improve their gameplay, and their English language developed naturally as a by-product of that desire to improve. Children combined cognitive, social, affective, and motivational language learning strategies to build their English language skills, displaying impressive levels of self-regulated learning. This study concludes by suggesting that teachers can harness children’s intrinsic motivation for video gaming by integrating elements of their gaming worlds into the classroom. The study aims to contribute to the field by offering insights into how informal digital activities can enhance English language teaching to young learners.

title: Virtual reality for language learning
text_snippet: Virtual reality for language learning Abstract Virtual reality (VR) creates 3D environments that immerse users in digital worlds, ranging from fully immersive experiences using headsets to non-immersive ones on PCs and mobile phones. While VR has been successfully applied in fields like manufacturing and paramedicine, its use in language teaching and learning is still developing. Research on VR in language education highlights benefits such as increased motivation and engagement, contextualised learning, and improved learning outcomes through embodied cognition. However, challenges remain, including a lack of familiarity with VR among teachers and learners, limited time and resources for experimentation, and the issue of cybersickness. This paper explores practical applications of VR in language learning by introducing VR apps that can be used to enhance language education. It also offers practical suggestions for teachers interested in using VR effectively in their classrooms and suggests potential future advancements in VR for education.

title: ELF awareness and learners’ realities: a response to Éva Illés
text_snippet: ELF awareness and learners’ realities: a response to Éva Illés Abstract This response article addresses key misconceptions about the scope, aims, and practical implications of ELF-aware pedagogy, as presented in Éva Illés’ article ‘Ways of implementing ELF in the classroom’. We argue that her critique of the ELF-aware pedagogy is unfounded and that her suggestions about integrating ELF-informed activities that focus on individual learners’ linguistic, cognitive, and pragmatic use of ELF outside of their ELT environment have always been an integral component of the ELF-aware approach. We go on to explain that ELF-aware pedagogy focuses on learners’ holistic development as autonomous ELF users. Grounded in transformative learning theory, it integrates learners’ sociocultural realities, facilitating the development of their communication skills and fostering critical reflection. We contend that this approach not only supports engagement with ELF complexity but also empowers learners to re-define their identities within inclusive, learner-centred classrooms.

title: The impact of English language test choice for higher education admissions in the UK: perceptions of key stakeholders
text_snippet: The impact of English language test choice for higher education admissions in the UK: perceptions of key stakeholders Abstract This study investigates the complexities surrounding English language test choices for Higher Education (HE) admissions in the United Kingdom, focusing on the implications for institutional practices, student success, and stakeholder perceptions. Amid an evolving landscape, exacerbated by the pandemic, universities have faced challenges in ensuring that English language tests adequately measure the academic language proficiency required for international students. Drawing from desk-based research of 50 UK universities and a survey involving 67 HE personnel, the study highlights disparities in test acceptance, decision-making processes, and the validity of emerging at-home tests. Findings reveal concerns over test reliability, academic preparedness, and the impacts on student well-being and institutional reputation. The paper advocates for the development of robust evaluation frameworks, enhanced language assessment literacy, and targeted support services to address these challenges. By adopting evidence-based approaches, universities can better balance accessibility with maintaining academic standards, ultimately supporting international students’ success.

title: Language assessment as a source of emotion labour: voices from Nepali EFL teachers
text_snippet: Language assessment as a source of emotion labour: voices from Nepali EFL teachers Abstract Despite ample evidence on the impact of emotion labor on English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers’ burnout and retention, scant attention has been paid to assessment factors in their emotion labor. Thus, this study explored the role of formative and summative assessment practices in teachers’ emotion labor. Thirteen Nepali EFL teachers completed narrative frames and participated in semi-structured interviews. Data analysis using MAXQDA revealed that the teachers experienced significant emotion labor from challenges in meeting parental and school expectations, the strain of assessment and feedback, and balancing the demands of formative and summative assessment. Furthermore, teachers reported excessive stress arising from social pressures for academic success, emotional impacts from fluctuating student performance, and the extensive burden of assessment tasks. The conflict between curriculum demands, assessment practices, and institutional pressures further exacerbated their stress. The findings underscore the need for systemic support to alleviate teachers’ emotional burden and improve assessment practices.

title: Creating multilingual schoolscapes in restrictive ELT contexts
text_snippet: Creating multilingual schoolscapes in restrictive ELT contexts Abstract Restrictions on languages for instruction in classrooms or in local settings can marginalise minority languages and perpetuate monolingual practices. Nevertheless, teachers in such contexts may still actively create opportunities to engage their students’ full linguistic repertoires in the linguistic landscape of their classrooms, also known as the schoolscape This article explores how two ELT educators redesigned their physical, and aural landscapes to challenge and resist prevalent, top-down monolingual mandates in K-12 education in Israel and the United States. These examples demonstrate how teachers may creatively utilise semiotic and sensorial repertoires to disrupt dominant narratives and promote educational equity in linguistically restrictive and often socio-politically tense ELT contexts. While these examples are context-specific, ELT professionals may adapt them to challenge monolingual ideologies in their own local contexts, as part of contributing to a more equitable global educational landscape.

title: Bridging extramural English and formal instruction
text_snippet: Bridging extramural English and formal instruction Abstract This article reports on a study of Norwegian hybrid general study and vocational students’ extramural English (EE) engagement and vocabulary acquisition, the synergies they saw between vocabulary gained in this way and the linguistic demands of the classroom and workplace, and how they sought to leverage their EE engagement to support classroom learning. Semi-structured, face-to-face group interviews, together with language diaries, were used to gather data. The findings revealed that EE activities facilitated general and informal vocabulary learning, yet provided minimal exposure to academic and vocational registers. Participants emphasised the critical role of explicit in-class instruction for mastering academic and vocational vocabulary, rejecting the wholesale integration of EE into the language curriculum. Instead, they advocated for specific EE content and extending mandatory English instruction beyond the current one-year requirement to consolidate domain-specific language skills. The study challenges assumptions that EE inherently complements formal instruction.

title: Teacher input prompts and student listening strategies in EMI classes
text_snippet: Teacher input prompts and student listening strategies in EMI classes Abstract Language learning strategies have been of interest to researchers and educators alike for half a century. Recent research seeks to reinterpret and further theorise strategies, questioning whether strategies have to be self-regulated, or can instead be other-regulated. This study draws on data from a naturalistic English Medium Instruction classroom to investigate how learners use listening strategies when comprehending teacher input. Lesson observations and stimulated recall interviews with eight students provided in-depth data on how students’ strategies were prompted by the teacher (e.g. teacher asking students to recall their prior knowledge) during classroom interaction. The findings empirically support state-of-the-art thinking in the field that listening strategies do not have to be self-regulated and can be prompted by the other. Pedagogical implications are discussed in terms of the interactive nature of learners’ strategy use in relation to teacher input, and how teachers can prompt learners’ use of strategies to facilitate uptake.

title: Are English for tourism textbooks ELF-informed?
text_snippet: Are English for tourism textbooks ELF-informed? Abstract The current role of English as global lingua franca has heightened the need for a reconceptualization of how the language is taught and learnt. Most interactions in English today occur in lingua franca settings with multilingual speakers from a wide variety of contexts. Nonetheless, most ELT textbooks solely focus on a native-speaker model both in terms of language and culture. A great number of studies have focused on the extent to which the linguistic and cultural perspectives brought about by ELF and World Englishes research have permeated into textbooks; however, rather less attention has been paid on how they have been incorporated in English for Specific Purposes (henceforth, ESP) textbooks. To this end, this study explores the extent to which an ELF-aware perspective is present in seven English for tourism textbooks. On the whole, the results show a prevalence of Inner-circle linguistic and cultural content.

title: The impact of automated writing evaluation on writing gains
text_snippet: The impact of automated writing evaluation on writing gains Abstract This study examines the effectiveness of ChatGPT in improving English writing skills for English as a foreign language (EFL) students over a nine-week intervention. Specifically, it explores ChatGPT’s impact on syntactic and lexical complexity—key dimensions of writing development. The study compares two groups: one receiving teacher feedback alone and another using ChatGPT alongside teacher feedback. Participants included 105 first-year university students in Belgium, divided into these two groups. Results indicate that while ChatGPT significantly affects text length and complexity, it does not necessarily lead to sustained writing improvement. This finding is crucial for researchers and educators integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools with traditional teaching, as it refines current insights into generative AI’s educational potential. The study underscores the need for balanced approaches in writing instruction, where AI complements rather than replaces human feedback, ensuring that short-term benefits translate into long-term writing proficiency for EFL learners.

title: Addressing linguacultural competencies in business English pedagogy
text_snippet: Addressing linguacultural competencies in business English pedagogy Abstract Internationally operating business professionals communicate using English as a business lingua franca (BELF). As BELF communication crosses national borders and includes multiple languages and cultural groups, linguacultural competence is a critical aspect of successful BELF communication. In this study, we derived specific linguacultural competencies (LCCs) required for such communication from the literature and double-checked them with twelve business professionals and two business English teachers. The LCCs were then used to develop a questionnaire to gather the perceptions of ninety business professionals. The results of the survey revealed that all the identified LCCs were deemed essential, with no significant differences between region-based subgroups of respondents. Further, the study highlighted the importance of three components of LCC (knowledge, skill/strategies, and attitudes) to both real-world communication and pedagogy. These findings have important pedagogical implications for developing the LCCs of business professionals and creating a more connected, empathetic, and understanding international business environment.

title: Leveraging transnational identities of refugee-background students
text_snippet: Leveraging transnational identities of refugee-background students Abstract This study examines a North Korean refugee-background student’s experiences of learning and using English across different transnational contexts. Through semi-structured interviews conducted over a four-year period, the study explores the interplay between the participant’s transnational identities and his English-learning trajectory. The results illustrate how the participant leverages his transnational identities as assets, utilizing his unique experiences and perspectives to enhance his English skills and broaden his global outlook. The findings strongly support inclusive, culturally responsive English language programs that harness diverse linguistic backgrounds, empowering refugee-background students by recognizing their unique strengths and experiences. Based on the current findings, we propose reconceptualizing refugee-background students in the English classroom through a lens of transnationalism and asset-based pedagogy.

title: Four leadership innovation praxes: A synthesis of accomplished school leaders’ approaches
text_snippet: Four leadership innovation praxes: A synthesis of accomplished school leaders’ approaches Educational leaders face increasing pressure to innovate while maintaining coherence and equity, yet existing leadership traditions require more practice-supported accounts of innovation under constraint. This qualitative study examines how accomplished leaders address these challenges through semi-structured interviews with 10 nationally recognised U.S. PK-12 school leaders, including principals, superintendents and a state commissioner of education. Four interconnected themes emerged: Systems Design and Alignment, Stakeholder Engagement and Collective Ownership, Capacity Building and Distributed Leadership, and Relational Trust and Organisational Culture. Grounded in Freire's concept of praxis, these themes constitute the Four Leadership Innovation Praxes (FLIP), a practice-grounded heuristic, not a prescriptive framework or validated tool, but an interpretive lens organising four interrelated praxes through which accomplished leaders navigate innovation under constraint. FLIP offers a way of engaging the knowing–doing gap in educational leadership by linking conceptual coherence with situated, reflective practice. The implications include reorienting leadership preparation toward experiential learning and fostering policy contexts that enable rather than constrain innovation.

title: Holding schools together: Leadership as organizational repair under conditions of institutional fragility
text_snippet: Holding schools together: Leadership as organizational repair under conditions of institutional fragility Dominant models of school leadership conceptualize effectiveness in terms of improvement, development, and organizational growth, typically assuming institutional stability and sufficient capacity. However, many schools operate under conditions of sustained institutional fragility, characterized by cumulative policy demands, constrained resources, and limited buffering capacity. In such contexts, the central challenge of leadership shifts from enabling improvement to preventing organizational erosion and sustaining coordinated functioning. This study introduces organizational repair as a theoretical lens to examine the relational and emotional work through which leaders stabilize organizational coherence, professional commitment, and coordinated action under continuous strain. A qualitative-dominant mixed-methods multiple-case study was conducted in five public primary schools in Cyprus (n = 124), combining whole-network social network analysis with interviews, observations, and document analysis. The findings demonstrate that leadership under sustained fragility is enacted through three interrelated mechanisms: trust stabilization, emotional containment, and the redistribution of relational labor. title: Instructional leadership and student achievement in a centrally regulated system: A school-level test of academic optimism as an organisational pathway
text_snippet: Instructional leadership and student achievement in a centrally regulated system: A school-level test of academic optimism as an organisational pathway This study examines how instructional leadership is associated with school-level student achievement within a centrally regulated education system, positioning academic optimism as a key organisational mediator. Rooted in the indirect-effects perspective, the study investigates whether leadership relates to student outcomes by shaping a collective belief system defined by academic emphasis, collective efficacy, and trust. Data were collected from 934 teachers across 205 Anatolian high schools in Türkiye and merged with official achievement records for 41,847 tenth-grade students. School-level structural equation modelling, controlling for family socioeconomic status, reveals a theoretically anticipated competitive mediation pattern. Instructional leadership shows a statistically significant positive indirect association with achievement through academic optimism, while its residual direct association with achievement is negative. These results suggest a dual process in centralised high-stakes accountability contexts: principals indirectly promote achievement by cultivating an optimistic academic culture, whereas the negative direct path reflects supervisory escalation in response to performance pressure. title: Only for school heroes? A qualitative study of Argentine school principals under structural constraints
text_snippet: Only for school heroes? A qualitative study of Argentine school principals under structural constraints This article examines school leadership under structural constraints in Argentina. Drawing primarily on 128 semistructured interviews with primary and secondary principals, and using regulatory analysis and official statistics for contextual triangulation, it analyzes how principals lead when distributed leadership is limited by hierarchical governance, concentrated accountability, weak inter-institutional support, scarce organizational time, and fragile collaborative structures. The findings show hybrid configurations in which collaboration, informal teacher leadership, and relational support coexist with individualized responsibility and institutional solitude. The article distinguishes educational infrastructure, understood as the broader institutional environment of leadership, from structural constraints, understood as restrictive conditions experienced by principals as relatively fixed limits on action. It argues that heroic leadership is not an individual trait or moral exception, but a structural effect of systems that depend on principals to compensate for regulatory, organizational, and relational deficits.

title: School leaders’ crisis management responsibilities in the shadows of safety: A content analysis of educational leadership standards across the United States
text_snippet: School leaders’ crisis management responsibilities in the shadows of safety: A content analysis of educational leadership standards across the United States School leaders are expected to prepare for, respond to, and lead recovery efforts after a crisis that disrupts the normal operation of schools. However, empirical evidence suggests that principals may be unprepared to fulfill these responsibilities. Given the influence of standards on what principals learn and are expected to know, this study examines the educational leadership standards for 49 states and the District of Columbia to understand the extent to which, and how, they frame school leaders’ crisis management expectations. Through summative content analysis, we find minimal attention to these functions, with only 10 states explicitly referencing crisis or crisis management. A second key finding is the predominant framing of crisis management as ensuring school safety, with an emphasis on physical safety. We offer implications for discussions about principals’ crisis management responsibilities for consideration in future revisions of national and state standards. We also highlight implications for preparation programs, emphasizing the need for curricula that address required crisis management functions and competencies.

title: Student-centered leadership in higher education: Perspectives from academic Department Heads
text_snippet: Student-centered leadership in higher education: Perspectives from academic Department Heads Student engagement, learning outcomes, and competency development have garnered growing attention in higher education. However, academic leaders often face challenges in fostering holistic student learning while also enhancing student career prospects. Drawing on student-centered leadership (SCL) theory, this study examines how university Department Heads (DHs) facilitate student learning and development, and explores the extent to which the K-12 SCL model is transferable to higher education contexts. The case study draws on semistructured interviews with eight DHs in a Canadian university. Data were analyzed using abductive reasoning. Findings show that DHs acted as operational actors who sought to improve learning outcomes by integrating high-impact practices into, and enhancing the quality of, teaching and curricula. A deep analysis of the findings suggests that DHs were required to make trade-offs between administrative compliance and student-centered practices, as their professional agency was constrained by intersecting cultural, structural, and resource-related factors. title: Should I stay or should I go? Quantitative analysis of school leaders’ intentions to transfer or exit through the lens of the job demands–resources model
text_snippet: Should I stay or should I go? Quantitative analysis of school leaders’ intentions to transfer or exit through the lens of the job demands–resources model This study investigated the differential effects of school leaders’ intention to leave the school (transfer) or the profession (exit) using the job demands–resources model as a theoretical lens. Working overtime and the socioeconomic status of the school were considered job demands, while psychological safety was regarded as a job resource, and self-efficacy was categorized as a personal resource. Structural equation modeling was performed on a sample of 956 school leaders with transfer intentions and 2179 school leaders with exit intentions from across Switzerland. The analysis revealed that job demands were not significant predictors of transfer or exit intentions, or job satisfaction. However, psychological safety had a significant, direct and negative effect on transfer and exit intentions, as well as a significant indirect effect via job satisfaction. Self-efficacy not only had a significant indirect effect via job satisfaction on both intentions, but also a significant, direct and positive effect on transfer intentions. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of focusing on strengthening job resources rather than reducing job demands in the context of turnover of school leaders. title: The mediating role of adaptive expertise in the relationship between transformational leadership and teacher collaborative professionalism in Tanzanian schools
text_snippet: The mediating role of adaptive expertise in the relationship between transformational leadership and teacher collaborative professionalism in Tanzanian schools This mixed-methods study explores whether adaptive expertise mediates the relationship between transformational leadership and teacher collaborative professionalism in Tanzanian secondary schools – a resource-constrained context where imported leadership models often produce disappointing results. Surveying 439 teachers across 15 schools, with follow-up principal interviews, the study uses structural equation modelling and multi-group analysis. Adaptive expertise does mediate the leadership–collaboration link, but only through two of its four dimensions. Knowledge and innovation serve as positive pathways: when principals build teachers’ shared knowledge and encourage collaborative innovation, teachers report greater collaboration. In contrast, metacognition (reflective thinking) remains a private activity that does not translate into collaborative practice, and autonomy (freedom to act) benefits only teachers with master's degrees, not the majority. The direct effect of transformational leadership on collaboration is negative, suggesting that inspirational rhetoric without material support and follow-through may actually trigger teacher disengagement. title: How does principals’ job crafting relate to leadership for learning? Emotional regulation as a mediating mechanism in a centralised education system
text_snippet: How does principals’ job crafting relate to leadership for learning? Emotional regulation as a mediating mechanism in a centralised education system This study examines how principals’ job crafting relates to leadership for learning through emotional regulation. Although leadership for learning is central to school improvement, limited attention has been paid to the proactive work-design behaviours that support its implementation. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory, we propose that principals who actively craft their jobs by increasing structural resources and seeking challenging demands are better able to regulate their emotions, which may support their capacity to enact leadership for learning (LfL) practices. Using survey data from 698 principals working in K-12 schools across 14 provinces in Türkiye, we employed latent structural equation modelling to test direct and indirect relationships. The findings indicated that principal job crafting is positively related to LfL and that emotional regulation partially mediates this relationship. By integrating job crafting into the leadership for learning framework and identifying emotional regulation as a mediating mechanism, this study contributes to the global school leadership literature by explaining how leadership for learning may be supported by proactive work design and psychological resources in centralised education sy

title: Teacher leadership and school improvement in Asia: A systematic review
text_snippet: Teacher leadership and school improvement in Asia: A systematic review This systematic review synthesizes 74 empirical studies to examine the role of teacher leadership in school improvement across Asian contexts. Teacher leadership is conceptualized as a dynamic, relational process through which teachers influence colleagues and school culture to support instructional improvement. Following PRISMA guidelines, the review identifies three core dimensions: leadership enactment, enabling organizational conditions and school improvement outcomes and proposes a conceptual model of their interaction. The findings indicate that professional growth and change agency are the most frequently reported outcomes while principal support is a key enabling condition for teacher leadership. The review further highlights that teacher leadership in Asian contexts is shaped by cultural values such as collective harmony and relational trust. However, the evidence reveals a lack of longitudinal research and a need for culturally attuned leadership models that reflect Asian educational contexts. These findings provide a strategic roadmap for policymakers and practitioners to institutionalize leadership pathways, strengthen professional learning communities and foster collaborative school cultures that support sustainable school improvement. title: Distributed leadership of middle leaders in a Singapore polytechnic
text_snippet: Distributed leadership of middle leaders in a Singapore polytechnic Despite growing studies on distributed leadership, significant gaps persist in understanding how it manifests in higher education, particularly within Asian hierarchical institutional settings. Limited research has examined middle leaders’ lived experiences in enacting distributed leadership. This study examines distributed leadership practices of middle leaders in a Singapore polytechnic, exploring their perceived experiences, affordances, and constraints within a higher education setting. Using phenomenological methodology, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 Course Leaders. Findings revealed that middle leaders enacted distributed leadership through informal role assignments based on expertise, networking with stakeholders to create leadership development opportunities, facilitating shared decision-making, and fostering collective engagement. Key affordances included domain knowledge proficiency, stakeholder relationships, and operational familiarity, whilst key constraints encompassed inadequate leadership preparation, complex stakeholder management and administrative burdens. The study reconceptualises distributed leadership as a pragmatically bounded practice shaped by hierarchical institutional structures and cultural values, rather than diminished by them.

title: Relational infrastructure and distributed leadership: A longitudinal study of school system development
text_snippet: Relational infrastructure and distributed leadership: A longitudinal study of school system development Distributed leadership in schools has attracted substantial research attention, yet how the organizational conditions it requires actually develop over time remains poorly understood. This article addresses that question through a 3-year longitudinal study of school system development in a Swedish municipality, engaging principals, deputy principals, and middle leaders across an entire school system in sustained collective work. We introduce the concept of relational infrastructure—the trust networks, dialogue practices, and shared meaning-making processes that enable collaborative leadership to emerge and endure—and propose a four-phase process model showing how these conditions develop from individual experimentation to organizational culture. Relational infrastructure extends the educational infrastructure perspective by theorizing relational and cultural dimensions that existing frameworks identify but do not fully develop. The study contributes a processual account of distributed leadership development at system level, showing how relational infrastructure is built through deliberate developmental work within a stable formal architecture, how it deepens across phases, and how it can erode when the organizational conditions sustaining it are disrupted. title: Coping under fire: Street-level school leadership in wartime
text_snippet: Coping under fire: Street-level school leadership in wartime During prolonged wartime conditions, school principals must lead their communities while mediating pressures from multiple stakeholders, allocating scarce resources, and interpreting ambiguous policy goals under ongoing uncertainty. This study examines how principals cope with the challenges they face during prolonged wartime conditions. Drawing on the street-level bureaucracy framework and Tummers and colleagues’ typology of coping among public professionals, we conceptualize coping as a relational and discretionary process through which principals continuously negotiate competing institutional and emotional demands. Using 60 semistructured, in-depth interviews with Israeli school principals in the wake of October 7, 2023 and the ensuing war, we identify four coping movements: moving toward stakeholders, moving away from stakeholders, moving against stakeholders, and dynamically shifting between stakeholders. The findings demonstrate that coping under prolonged wartime conditions is not a stable or isolated response to external pressures, but rather a fluid, multidirectional, and politically embedded process that emerges through interactions with diverse stakeholders. title: Principal leadership styles and school violence: The mediating role of teachers’ professional commitment in Israeli Arab schools
text_snippet: Principal leadership styles and school violence: The mediating role of teachers’ professional commitment in Israeli Arab schools School violence is shaped not only by student behavior but also by broader social dynamics and school level conditions, making leadership, and teacher-related factors especially important for understanding safer school climates. This study examines the direct and indirect associations (via teachers’ professional commitment) of transformational and transactional leadership with school violence. To reduce common method bias, data were collected from two sources: 213 senior management team members (SMT) and 213 teachers who were not SMT members, drawn from 71 middle and high schools in the Arab educational system in Israel. Data was aggregated at the school level of analysis. Structural equation modeling and bootstrapping analysis indicated that teachers’ professional commitment functions as a mediating mechanism linking both leadership styles to school violence. Higher professional commitment appears to enhance the effectiveness of principals’ leadership practices, supporting stronger leadership processes at the school level and contributing to a safer, more positive learning climate. Implications for theory and practice are discussed.

title: Not all stressors are equal: Using ecological theory to examine systems that predict stress and mental health in principals
text_snippet: Not all stressors are equal: Using ecological theory to examine systems that predict stress and mental health in principals Stressors in the principalship are plentiful, but few studies have examined their differential impacts on work-stress and mental health, particularly from a systems perspective. Guided by Lazarus and Folkman's occupational stress theory and Bronfenbrenner's ecological theory, we conducted an embedded mixed-method design with a quantitative-dominant crossover analysis for hierarchical regression to identify emergent stressors, the systems from which they originate, and whether stressor systems, cumulatively and differentially, predict negative psychological outcomes including work-stress, anxiety, and depression. We identified ten thematic stressors that were organized into five systems based on proximity to the principalship and degree of control: nanosystem, microsystem, macrosystem, exosystem, and chronosystem. In our sample, principals reported high work-stress, moderate anxiety, and mild to moderate depression symptoms. Regression analyses showed that the cumulative number of stressors significantly predict work-stress. However, only system-level stressors, especially nanosystem stressors, predicted anxiety, and depression symptoms. title: Enacting subject leadership as practice: Primary science and curriculum marginalisation in English primary schools
text_snippet: Enacting subject leadership as practice: Primary science and curriculum marginalisation in English primary schools Subject leadership in primary schools is increasingly recognised as important for curriculum quality, yet little is known about how subject leadership is enacted as practice in marginalised curriculum areas such as science within high-accountability systems. This study explores how primary science subject leaders in English schools understand and enact their leadership role within a high-stakes accountability context. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with science subject leaders across school contexts, the study adopts a leadership-as-practice and sensemaking theoretical lens to examine leadership as situated, relational, and shaped by organisational and policy conditions. Findings indicate that science leadership is enacted primarily through influence rather than formal authority, with leaders engaging in advocacy, relationship-building and ongoing negotiation to secure time, status and legitimacy for science within a crowded curriculum. Participants’ leadership practices were shaped by accountability pressures and the prioritisation of English and Mathematics, requiring leaders to respond creatively to inspection signals while sustaining teacher confidence and curriculum coherence. title: Leadership development of university teachers in China: A mixed-methods model development and validation study
text_snippet: Leadership development of university teachers in China: A mixed-methods model development and validation study This study develops and validates a contextually grounded model of teacher leadership in Chinese higher education, addressing a gap in the literature dominated by school-based and Western-centric frameworks. Drawing on mixed methods, including grounded theory and confirmatory factor analysis, data were collected from 352 university faculty members across multiple Chinese provinces. This study employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design: (1) a qualitative phase (in-depth interviews) to generate context-specific dimensions and indicators of teacher leadership; and (2) a quantitative phase (survey) to test the emergent model via exploratory factor analysis/confirmatory factor analysis. The qualitative phase was conducted in October–November 2023; the quantitative survey took place from November 2023 to February 2024. The resulting four-dimensional model encompasses moral leadership, teaching leadership, research leadership, and team leadership. Findings reveal that moral and teaching leadership dominate faculty perceptions, reflecting the cultural importance of ethical conduct and pedagogical engagement in the Chinese academic tradition. title: Mediating ambiguity: Principals’ sense-making and instructional leadership in curriculum reform enactment
text_snippet: Mediating ambiguity: Principals’ sense-making and instructional leadership in curriculum reform enactment Effective leadership by school principals is reported to involve shaping school cultures, fostering collaboration, allocating resources, and motivating teachers’ attitudes which results in (in-)directly impacting student learning. While the literature recommends a move toward collective and distributed processes of sense-making, the role of the school principal and their respective leadership practices in the context of curriculum reform is still largely underrepresented. Using an integrated framework of policy enactment, sense-making and instructional leadership, this article explores how school principals interpreted curriculum reform at lower secondary level in the Republic of Ireland and how these interpretations translated into leadership practices. This qualitative study, part of a larger national 4-year longitudinal study, interviewed 65 secondary school principals approximately a decade after implementation regarding their experiences of leading Junior Cycle reforms. Our findings reveal that in contested reform contexts, instructional leadership dimensions of programme management and climate-building functionally collapse into reciprocal practices shaped by principals’ diagnostic assessment of organisational readiness. title: Governing teacher well-being in international policy discourse: Problem representation, accountability, and the individualisation of care
text_snippet: Governing teacher well-being in international policy discourse: Problem representation, accountability, and the individualisation of care Teacher well-being has become a prominent concern in contemporary education policy, yet it is rarely treated as a structural or ethical responsibility in its own right. Instead, it is frequently mobilised instrumentally through its assumed effects on performance, retention, and system efficiency. This article examines how teacher well-being is constituted as a policy problem within internationally circulating education policy discourse. Drawing on Bacchi’s What's the Problem Represented to be? (WPR) approach, and informed by White's relational conceptualisation of well-being, it develops an interpretive policy analysis of influential texts through which it is made visible and governed across contexts. The analysis shows that well-being is predominantly represented as an individual responsibility, to be secured through resilience, self-regulation, and emotional self-management, rather than as a condition shaped by organisational and material arrangements. title: Meso-level education governance: The rise and fall of regional improvement collaboratives in Scotland
text_snippet: Meso-level education governance: The rise and fall of regional improvement collaboratives in Scotland Academic research has increasingly prioritised learner-centred reform, often overlooking the political dynamics that shape how reforms unfold. Large-scale change frequently falters because technocratic approaches fail to account for these complex political processes, while neoliberal, performance-driven agendas reinforce top-down reforms that marginalise the cultural and relational dimensions essential for meaningful improvement. This article examines the politics of education reform in Scotland through the creation and dissolution of the Regional Improvement Collaboratives (RICs), established after the 2016 Governance Review. Although the Review aimed to develop a more empowered, school-led system grounded in subsidiarity, the RICs exposed persistent tensions between local autonomy and central oversight and highlighted the dominance of structural over cultural change. Documentary analysis shows how policy narratives shaped governance and practice, revealing challenges in collaboration, the limiting effects of restricted funding and the impact of uneven evaluation and shifting national priorities. title: From heroic leadership myth to street-level management: School principals’ experiences of sensemaking and creative insubordination under incomplete autonomy
text_snippet: From heroic leadership myth to street-level management: School principals’ experiences of sensemaking and creative insubordination under incomplete autonomy The normative ‘heroic leadership’ discourse positions school principals as transformative visionaries, yet in highly centralised systems this narrative breaks down, giving rise to the twin challenges of ‘incomplete autonomy’ and ‘street-level management’. This phenomenological study examines how 15 principals in Türkiye's centralised education system respond to structural disempowerment: how they make sense of authority gaps and develop creative insubordination practices to keep their schools running. Data were collected through in-depth interviews and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenological reduction. Three themes emerged: (1) Structural Siege and the Experience of Incomplete Autonomy, (2) Sensemaking and Creative Insubordination Under the Grip of Incomplete Autonomy, and (3) Lack of Psychological Safety and the Bureaucratic Vice. Principals are not passive implementers; when rigid regulations clash with urgent educational needs, they act – moving along a continuum from legitimate discretion to creative insubordination – to prevent schools from grinding to a halt.
