title: Tracing Interconnected Development in Self‐Directed L2 Learning: Journal Writing as a Window Into L2 Change in a Longitudinal Case Study
text_snippet: Tracing Interconnected Development in Self‐Directed L2 Learning: Journal Writing as a Window Into L2 Change in a Longitudinal Case Study ABSTRACT This exploratory longitudinal case study investigates the one‐year L2 English development of a working adult engaged in self‐directed learning, focusing on the activities, resources, and contexts that influenced the participant's progress. Drawing on longitudinal quantitative and qualitative data, journal entries and monthly essays were collected and analyzed, along with interviews, surveys, session notes, and email exchanges to explore the participant's perspectives on L2 learning and selected learning approaches and resources. This case illustrates the dynamic, non‐linear nature of the participant's L2 development, including the interconnected influence of learning resources, the emergence of syntactically complex structures, and shifts in perceptions of English in relation to diverse learning materials. These outcomes suggest that, in this case, L2 development emerged through interacting cognitive, affective, and contextual factors rather than linear cause–effect relationships. Given the single‐case design, the findings offer case‐based insights into the dynamic processes underlying self‐directed L2 learning.

title: Agency‐Structure Dynamics in the Linguistic Landscape of a Global Mega‐Event: The 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics
text_snippet: Agency‐Structure Dynamics in the Linguistic Landscape of a Global Mega‐Event: The 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics ABSTRACT This article advances an agency‐structure perspective on linguistic landscapes (LLs) by examining the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics as a global mega‐event held during the pandemic. Drawing on geosemiotic analysis of multilingual signs and displays, it conceptualizes the LL not only as a collection of texts but as a social and discursive space in which actors’ practices and institutional arrangements are mutually constitutive. The findings show how the Chinese government, as the primary organizer, macro‐designed the visual‐linguistic environment to comply with long‐standing Olympic conventions and address the need for COVID‐19 prevention measures, while projecting China's cultural confidence on the world stage. Meanwhile, participants, audiences and individuals exercised agency within the event's time‐space structures, inserting their own signs and messages into public view. By theorizing the LL as the negotiated outcome of structural forces and agentic action, this study highlights how global sporting events simultaneously reproduce the Olympic legacy and generate context‐specific innovations, thereby extending LL research beyond the static description of signs toward a deeper understanding of the agency‐structure dynamics that shape multilingual public space.

title: Sustaining Translanguaging Pedagogies: Teacher‐Learners’ Approaches Toward L2 Motivational Development in the Thai EFL Context
text_snippet: Sustaining Translanguaging Pedagogies: Teacher‐Learners’ Approaches Toward L2 Motivational Development in the Thai EFL Context ABSTRACT Although translanguaging research in applied linguistics has investigated the use of the first language and multilingualism in classroom‐based settings, few studies have illustrated how English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers enact and sustain translanguaging pedagogies in their second language (L2) teaching in the Thai EFL context. This paper reports on how four teacher‐learners (TLs) on an international teaching practicum integrated translanguaging into their teaching praxis while engaging in professional development to make sense of translanguaging pedagogies. Audio‐recorded dialogues between the authors and TLs were analyzed using interpretive phenomenological analysis. The analysis revealed how TLs’ teaching praxis (1) made sense of translanguaging, (2) negotiated pedagogical and relational boundaries of L1 use, and (3) built co‐learning spaces and engagement. Drawing on these findings, we argue sustained professional dialogue facilitates dialogic spaces where TLs can position and interrogate their teaching knowledge, linguistic identities, and accumulated learning and teaching experiences. These spaces encourage more nuanced understandings of translanguaging and prompt TLs to critically evaluate and potentially reconfigure their peda

title: Task Complexity Effects on Writing Processes and Correlations With Text Features
text_snippet: Task Complexity Effects on Writing Processes and Correlations With Text Features ABSTRACT Research on task complexity (TC) effects on second language (L2) text features is abundant and has contributed critical insights. Comparatively, less is known about how L2 writers respond cognitively to diverse TC conditions or about potential effects of such processing activity on the characteristics of the texts produced. To expand on previous research, this study examined (i) the effects of TC on L2 writers’ processing activity (operationalized as on‐line writing behaviors and macro writing processes) globally and across three time intervals; and (ii) any potential relationship of processing activity with text features (as measured by complexity, accuracy, and fluency indices). In an intra‐subject design study, 45 advanced L2 English users completed two argumentative writing tasks (in time‐compressed conditions) that varied in cognitive complexity, operationally defined as the provision of ±content support. Processing activity was captured with the keystroke logging software Inputlog, together with a self‐rating post‐task questionnaire. Results provided little evidence of TC effects on online writing behaviors but showed clearer differences in self‐reported macro‐writing processes, especially in the complex task condition. The analyses also indicated little evidence of TC effects on acc

title: L2 Chinese Grammatical Acquisition and Processing: A Substantive and Methodological Review
text_snippet: L2 Chinese Grammatical Acquisition and Processing: A Substantive and Methodological Review ABSTRACT This study presents a systematic review of 92 empirical studies on Chinese as a second language (CSL) in grammatical processing and development, synthesizing their substantive foci and methodological characteristics. The results reveal consistent scholarly attention to cross‐linguistic topics, with less focus on features that are distinctively salient in Chinese. Methodologically, studies most commonly relied on quantitative approaches and judgment tasks, while the use of online measures emerged only after 2014. We also identified several persistent challenges, including an overreliance on English‐speaking university students as participants, inconsistent proficiency assessment practices across studies, and limitations in transparent data reporting. In light of these limitations, we call for the adoption of a broader range of methodological tools, the inclusion of more diverse participants, varied research designs, and statistical techniques to enhance the rigor of CSL research and its contribution to the broader SLA field.

title: The “Pressure Trap”: A Mixed‐Methods Study of the L2 Motivational Self System and Academic Achievement in a Chinese Border Region
text_snippet: The “Pressure Trap”: A Mixed‐Methods Study of the L2 Motivational Self System and Academic Achievement in a Chinese Border Region ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between the L2 motivational self system and the academic achievement of junior English majors ( N = 243) within the socio‐geographic context of a border region in Southwest China. Employing a mixed‐methods design, the research utilized questionnaires, CET‐4 scores, and semi‐structured interviews to examine how different motivational self‐guides are associated with achievement patterns. Quantitative results from correlation and multiple regression analyses indicate that while the ideal L2 self and L2 learning experience are relatively strong positive predictors of CET‐4 performance, the ought‐to L2 self is significantly but modestly negatively associated with academic performance. Qualitative thematic analysis further illustrates these divergent motivational patterns: high achievers tended to report vivid future visions and positive pedagogical engagement, whereas some low achievers described external requirements, test‐induced anxiety, and perceived linguistic isolation in ways that this study interprets as a possible “pressure trap.” These findings suggest a nuanced role for the ought‐to L2 self, pointing to its potentially constraining association with achievement in high‐stakes testing environments

title: Contradiction and Construction: A Cultural‐Historical Activity Theory Analysis of a Chinese German Language Teacher's Professional Identity Formation With Generative AI
text_snippet: Contradiction and Construction: A Cultural‐Historical Activity Theory Analysis of a Chinese German Language Teacher's Professional Identity Formation With Generative AI ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, challenging teachers’ professional identities. Framed by third‐generation Cultural‐Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), this case study investigates how a secondary school German teacher in China developed her professional identity through GenAI integration. Findings revealed four levels of contradictions: primary (efficiency vs. competence), secondary (AI content vs. norms; skill gaps; AI vs. creativity), tertiary (traditional vs. AI‐supported pedagogy), and quaternary (tensions with colleagues and students). Resolving these contradictions transformed her identity across four dimensions. Epistemically, she became a reflective “quality gatekeeper.” Pedagogically, a human‐AI collaborative instructional designer. Relationally, a selective collaborator and digital literacy facilitator. Agentively, a reflective practitioner progressing from technology‐dependent anxiety to agentive practice. Her trajectory shifted from incremental adaptation toward emergent expansive learning. This study illuminates how language teachers can transform contradiction‐driven disruption into resilient, multidimensional professional identity dev

title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Support Secondary Students’ Cognitive Processes in Writing
text_snippet: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Support Secondary Students’ Cognitive Processes in Writing ABSTRACT While the benefits of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in supporting various cognitive processes in writing have been documented, most research has examined single stages of the writing process and focused on university students. This study addresses this gap by developing a domain‐specific GenAI chatbot and embedding it within a process‐based writing instruction (PBWI) program to explore its effectiveness and challenges in supporting secondary students’ Chinese writing across the three cognitive stages. A total of 100 first‐year secondary students participated in three conditions: the experimental group received PBWI with GenAI chatbot support, the control group received PBWI without GenAI, and the baseline group continued product‐based instruction. Data from writing tasks, questionnaires, and interviews were analyzed using a mixed‐methods approach. Results indicated that students reported benefits of the GenAI chatbot in supporting their writing across the three cognitive stages, as well as in both lower‐ and higher‐level aspects of writing. However, their performance outcomes did not significantly exceed those of the control group, likely owing to the added cognitive load of managing both PBWI and GenAI use. title: The Role of Positive and Negative Emotions in Resilience Among L2 Learners: A Three Level Meta‐Analytic Review
text_snippet: The Role of Positive and Negative Emotions in Resilience Among L2 Learners: A Three Level Meta‐Analytic Review ABSTRACT Second/foreign language (L2) learning is not solely a cognitive/linguistic acquisition process but includes mixed emotional experiences. Understanding how these emotional experiences relate to resilience could help our understanding of how learners navigate fluctuations in emotions when learning an L2. This study systematically synthesizes research on the relationship between emotions and resilience in L2 learners through a three‐level meta‐analysis of 13 primary studies ( N = 5,340) published between 2019 and 2025. The findings revealed two distinct emotional pathways to resilience: 1) positive emotions correlated positively with resilience (pooled r = 0.544; p r = ‒0.479; p

title: Evidence for the Development of L2 Grammar‐for‐Interaction: The Case of Wenti shi (“the Problem Is”) in L2 Chinese Interaction
text_snippet: Evidence for the Development of L2 Grammar‐for‐Interaction: The Case of Wenti shi (“the Problem Is”) in L2 Chinese Interaction ABSTRACT This study adopts an integrated framework combining Conversation Analysis for Second Language Acquisition (CA‐for‐SLA), Usage‐Based Linguistics (UBL), and Interactional Linguistics (IL) to trace the longitudinal development of an L2 Chinese learner's use of the construction wenti shi (“the problem is”, WTS) over a 15‐month period. Although quantitative analysis shows that the overall frequency of WTS did not increase substantially, qualitative findings reveal a clear developmental trajectory. Initially employed in its literal sense to present a factual problem, WTS was later mobilized to foreground an issue by upgrading the speaker's epistemic stance and projecting further talk. Building on this core function, two trajectories of functional expansion emerged: one oriented to managing topic transition and the other to prefacing contrasting stance and, eventually, disagreement. These functional developments were accompanied by changes in the construction's syntactic formatting, prosodic chunking, and sequential positioning, each unfolding at a different pace. title: Chinese University Students’ Motivation to Learn Greek: A Transnational Postdigital Exploration
text_snippet: Chinese University Students’ Motivation to Learn Greek: A Transnational Postdigital Exploration ABSTRACT Research on the motivation of learners of Languages Other Than English (LOTE) has grown steadily in recent years; however, most studies focus on classroom‐based activities and seldom consider how transnational experiences or digital practices contribute to motivational development. This study employs postdigital storytelling to qualitatively investigate how nine Chinese learners of Greek narratively construct their motivational selves throughout their Greek‐learning journeys informed by translanguaging and postdigital perspectives. Drawing on multiple data sources, including life‐history interviews, multimodal artifacts, and follow‐up interactions via email and social media, we conducted a multimodal thematic analysis to examine how LOTE motivational selves were constructed, expressed, and negotiated across digital and non‐digital linguistic activities. Findings show that participants’ motivation comprises an interplay of ought‐to, ideal, and multilingual selves. The ideal and multilingual selves were particularly activated during their transnational study experiences in Greece and through frequent social media engagement, where translanguaging served as a supportive mechanism for language development and intercultural identity formation. title: Take an Introductory Linguistics Course; It May Increase Your Language Learning Ability
text_snippet: Take an Introductory Linguistics Course; It May Increase Your Language Learning Ability ABSTRACT Can general linguistics knowledge be used to better learn a new language? This exploratory study is concerned with the potential advantageous transfer of general linguistics knowledge to the learning of a new, additional foreign language. We examine foreign language course letter grades (e.g., A–F) collected over 12 years at a private, predominantly STEM university in the United States. We first ask whether there is an association between taking a prior introductory linguistics class and the letter grade received in a first‐semester, beginner foreign language learning class. We indeed found a statistically significant association. Importantly, this association is seemingly unique to the linguistics course, as we found no such association between a control class (psychology) and foreign language learning letter grade. Moreover, this transfer did not work both ways. No association was found for linguistics letter grade and having taken a prior foreign language learning class. In a post‐hoc logistic regression analysis, we found that having taken a prior introduction to linguistics significantly increases the log‐odds of getting an “A” grade in a foreign language course. We interpret these results to mean that prior linguistics education on linguistics concepts and principles can advan

title: Translanguaging, Medium of Instruction and LX Learning Motivation
text_snippet: Translanguaging, Medium of Instruction and LX Learning Motivation ABSTRACT Multilingual education in post‐colonial societies challenges the traditional labelling of languages (e.g., L1, L2) in classroom contexts. For learners with complex linguistic repertoires, what might conventionally be called a ‘second language (L2)’ is often less a chronological L2 than an additional language (LX) that is organically integrated into the learner's repertoire and serves as a medium of learning. This recognition prompts a shift of focus from the target language promoted by the teacher to the complex processes experienced/engaged by the learner. In other words, L2 medium‐of‐instruction becomes LX medium‐of‐learning. This special issue seeks to break new paths by exploring the possibilities of this conceptual move in relation to language learning motivation (LLM). Research shows that L2 students without prior experience in L2 medium‐of‐instruction struggle with comprehension, participation and LLM, especially with demanding content. Translanguaging pedagogies support content and language learning, but their potentialities in LLM have not been explored fully. The special issue advocates centring students’ learning processes to address motivational challenges in LX‐medium‐of‐instruction. This special issue provides data‐driven insights into translanguaging as a mediator for LX motivational devel

title: From External Schema to Internal Tool: Navigating the Semantic Labyrinth of English Modals Through CL‐Informed Concept‐Based Language Instruction
text_snippet: From External Schema to Internal Tool: Navigating the Semantic Labyrinth of English Modals Through CL‐Informed Concept‐Based Language Instruction ABSTRACT This study investigated to what extent and how an integrated framework of cognitive linguistics (CL) and concept‐based language instruction (CBLI) supports the acquisition of English modal verbs among L2 learners. Using a quasi‐experimental design, the study compared a CL‐CBLI group ( n = 42) with a traditional‐CBLI group ( n = 40) and a control group ( n = 40) among intermediate‐level high school learners. Data from productive accuracy tests, conceptual development measures, and concurrent verbalizations were triangulated to evaluate instructional effectiveness and the process of internalization. Results suggest that the integrated CL‐CBLI approach significantly enhanced learners’ understanding of modality, evidenced by balanced accuracy across root and epistemic functions and superior long‐term retention compared to traditional descriptive methods. These findings indicate that providing a scientifically motivated orienting basis through force dynamics allows for the development of a unified and durable cognitive tool for L2 meaning‐making.

title: Edutainment Through Translanguaging Practices: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis of Short‐Form English Instructional Videos on Douyin
text_snippet: Edutainment Through Translanguaging Practices: A Multimodal Discourse Analysis of Short‐Form English Instructional Videos on Douyin ABSTRACT Recent research in applied linguistics has increasingly attended to translanguaging practices in digitally mediated contexts, yet relatively little is known about how translanguaging practices achieve edutainment within the context of the highly compressed short‐form videos as dynamic discourse on Douyin, China's localized counterpart to TikTok. Drawing on translanguaging theory and multimodal discourse analysis, the study analyzes a song video and a role‐play video for English language teaching. The findings show that content creators flexibly draw on diverse multilingual and multimodal resources. The orchestration of these translanguaging resources has created unique ways for the realization of edutainment in the song video and role‐play video, respectively. The findings also indicate that the use of diverse translanguaging resources in each type of video stimulates positive emotions. By providing the reconceptualization of edutainment, this study is positioned as a complementary study grounded in a specific empirical context. This study not only extends translanguaging scholarship into the dynamic context of short‐form videos on Douyin but also re‐examines the relationship between education and entertainment, enriching existing scholarl

title: EFL Learners’ Receptive Vocabulary Size and the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages: Estimates Across Levels
text_snippet: EFL Learners’ Receptive Vocabulary Size and the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages: Estimates Across Levels ABSTRACT The Common European Framework of Reference for languages (CEFR) is widely used as a reference for language teaching and learning. However, providing vocabulary size (VS) estimates is beyond the CEFR's original aim. Previous research has also shown that learners’ receptive VS is related to overall proficiency and to the four language skills. Nevertheless, the existing attempts to link receptive VS and the CEFR are very scarce and have not investigated vocabularies beyond the 5K level. The present study aims to fill these gaps by sampling 311 Spanish learners of English distributed across the six CEFR levels. Participants took the Oxford Placement Test (OPT) to know their proficiency level and the Vocabulary Size Test (VST), measuring receptive VS up to 14,000 word families. Results showed that these learners’ receptive VS ranged from 5,300 word families at the A1 level to 11,200 at the C2 level. Moreover, there were significant differences in VST scores depending on learners’ CEFR levels, although some adjacent‐level pairs failed to reach statistical significance. VST scores were also closely linked to OPT grammar scores, which explained 45.2% of the variance in receptive VS. The study sheds some light on the vocabulary descriptors of the CEFR an

title: Developing Chatbot Pragmatics Through Prompting Instruction in AI‐Assisted Communicative Practice
text_snippet: Developing Chatbot Pragmatics Through Prompting Instruction in AI‐Assisted Communicative Practice ABSTRACT This quasi‐experimental study examines the impact of short‐term prompting instruction on the communicative performance of Czech learners of English in human–chatbot interaction, conceptualizing their prompting behavior as a context‐specific manifestation of pragmatic competence. The study was conducted in two phases (September 2024 and May 2026) and included four groups of participants with varying chatbot experience. Participants with (experimental groups) and without (control groups) prior prompting instruction completed 20 communicative tasks of increasing complexity, during which four indicators of communication effectiveness were recorded: task completion rate, number of conversational turns, user satisfaction, and frequency of chatbot misunderstandings. The findings indicate that prompting instruction improves communication efficiency, particularly in higher‐complexity tasks, as reflected in fewer conversational turns and significantly reduced misunderstandings in human–chatbot interaction, alongside a modest, non‐significant advantage in task completion. More importantly, it facilitates a shift from the inference‐based pragmatic strategies typical of human–human communication toward more explicit forms of contextualization and communicative guidance. title: The Congruent and Incongruent Effects of Emotions on Willingness to Communicate: Insights From Polynomial Regression With Response Surface Analysis
text_snippet: The Congruent and Incongruent Effects of Emotions on Willingness to Communicate: Insights From Polynomial Regression With Response Surface Analysis ABSTRACT Although some prior studies examined how language learners’ enjoyment and anxiety affect L2 willingness to communicate (WTC), they predominantly employed linear statistical methods and largely ignored the possible curvilinear relationships. Adopting a polynomial regression with response surface analysis, the study intends to unveil the congruent and incongruent effects of two emotional factors (enjoyment and anxiety) on WTC among a total of 1,023 undergraduates from 21 universities in China. The results show that both linear and non‐linear effects are significant. Along the line of congruence, WTC displays a linear increasing trend when enjoyment and anxiety increase simultaneously and remain aligned. Along the incongruence line, WTC is higher when enjoyment is higher than anxiety, and as the degree of mismatch between enjoyment and anxiety increases, WTC exhibits a more pronounced upward trend. The study offers both theoretical and pedagogical insights when exploring the synergistic relationships between emotions and WTC. Theoretically, it moves beyond conventional correlation and regression methods by highlighting the co‐occurrence and interactions of the positive and negative emotions on WTC. It is also of pedagogical si

title: Exploring English Language Learners’ Vocabulary Knowledge and Usage When Speaking
text_snippet: Exploring English Language Learners’ Vocabulary Knowledge and Usage When Speaking ABSTRACT Vocabulary forms a fundamental component of speaking ability, as it enables speakers to convey meaning accurately, fluently, and effectively. Although the relationship between vocabulary and speaking has been investigated to some extent, gaps remain in understanding the link between learners’ vocabulary knowledge and their speaking proficiency, as well as how they deploy that knowledge in speaking performance. Drawing on speech production models, the present study examined the relationship between English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners’ vocabulary size knowledge and their speaking proficiency, as measured via a speaking task, and further investigated the extent of lexical richness in their speech. The results revealed a clear pattern in the contribution of vocabulary size knowledge to speaking proficiency, with aural vocabulary size showing the strongest predictive power. Findings further indicated that lexical diversity and sophistication emerged as important indicators. Overall, the findings suggested that speaking proficiency depends not only on the quantity of vocabulary knowledge, but also on how flexibly learners draw on diverse, semantically nuanced lexical resources. More proficient learners demonstrated the ability to balance diverse, sophisticated words with accessible, hi

title: Is Time Travel Possible? Accidental Signs as Sociolinguistic “Wormholes”
text_snippet: Is Time Travel Possible? Accidental Signs as Sociolinguistic “Wormholes” ABSTRACT Sociolinguistics primarily focuses on deliberately staged public signs, while relatively less attention has been given to ephemeral and non‐deliberate signs in urban environments. This study investigates “ accidental signs,” which are hidden historical texts suddenly exposed by unpredictable events. I argue that the accidental sign can be understood as a provisional phase in a sign's biography, a state in which an earlier textual layer returns to public visibility even though its display in the present was not intended. It aims to conceptualize accidental signs, categorize their emergence triggers, and analyze their sociolinguistic implications. Empirical evidence demonstrates that extreme weather, architectural decay, and urban redevelopment act as the primary catalysts for their sudden exposures. To theorize this phenomenon, this study introduces the physics concept of the “wormhole” as a heuristic metaphor for unstable, unpredictable, and site‐specific temporal rupture. This metaphor is also used to explain the illusion of time travel provoked by these signs. By conceptualizing this hidden side of societal sign phenomena, this study broadens the research areas of sociolinguistics and enriches sociolinguistic theories, particularly those related to linguistic landscapes.

title: How Genre Awareness Shapes L2 Academic Writing: Pathways Through Self‐Efficacy and Learning Engagement
text_snippet: How Genre Awareness Shapes L2 Academic Writing: Pathways Through Self‐Efficacy and Learning Engagement ABSTRACT This study addresses a gap in second language (L2) writing research by empirically examining how genre awareness—a cognitive concept derived from genre pedagogy—interacts with self‐efficacy (a motivational belief) and learning engagement (a multidimensional meta‐construct comprising vigor, dedication, and absorption) in relation to academic writing proficiency. Grounded in social cognitive theory and genre‐based frameworks, we propose a sequential mediation model in which genre awareness is linked to a chain effect through self‐efficacy and engagement. Data were collected from 736 English as a foreign language (EFL) learners using genre analysis tasks, validated writing assessments, and psychometric scales and analyzed with structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. The results showed that: (1) genre awareness had a direct association with writing ability (β = 0.447, p

title: Similar Semantic Category Distributions but Distinct Noun Choices in Nonacademic Second Language Writing of Graduate Students With Different Disciplinary Backgrounds: A Natural Language Processing‐Based Analysis
text_snippet: Similar Semantic Category Distributions but Distinct Noun Choices in Nonacademic Second Language Writing of Graduate Students With Different Disciplinary Backgrounds: A Natural Language Processing‐Based Analysis ABSTRACT The disciplinary background of second language (L2) writers can shape their writing style, including their lexical choices. This study examines lexical differences in nonacademic argumentative essays on the same topic by L2‐English graduate students with humanities‐related or science‐related majors. Using natural language processing (NLP) techniques, the study extracts nouns from these writers’ essays and classifies them into 21 semantic categories of the English UCREL Semantic Analysis System. Regression analyses show no significant difference in the distribution of the semantic categories between the two groups. However, a follow‐up keyness analysis reveals that their specific noun choices do differ significantly: The humanities students’ writing includes more nouns related to psychological and social ideas, while the science students’ writing utilizes more nouns referring to concrete objects. These findings suggest that even when L2 writers address a topic outside of their field, their disciplinary background plays a role in their noun choices, influencing how they express their ideas. title: Understanding Scaffolding in Peer Interactions Among Chinese University Students in an Intact EFL Classroom
text_snippet: Understanding Scaffolding in Peer Interactions Among Chinese University Students in an Intact EFL Classroom ABSTRACT While scaffolding has long been widely recognized as central to learning from a sociocultural perspective, prior studies have largely focused on identifying its characteristics or interactional strategies, leaving its interactional processes underexplored. This study adopts a conversation‐analysis (CA)‐informed sociocultural approach to investigate how scaffolding was interactionally enacted in peer group interactions among English as a foreign language (EFL) students at a Chinese university. The findings reveal two recurrent interactional routes to peer scaffolding: dynamic contingent support, through which diagnosis and assistance were interwoven within ongoing reasoning instead of being organized as a sequential ‘diagnosis‐then‐support’ process and thinking with divergent perspectives, through which alternative viewpoints were interactionally accommodated and assimilated into shared mediational resources. The study advances our understanding of scaffolding by specifying its micro‐interactional foundations and it details the pedagogical implications of this understanding for efforts to facilitate productive peer discussions in university EFL classrooms.

title: How Technology Affordances Foster Continuance Intention in English Speaking Practice with AI‐Based Conversational Agents: A Stimulus‐Organism‐Response Perspective
text_snippet: How Technology Affordances Foster Continuance Intention in English Speaking Practice with AI‐Based Conversational Agents: A Stimulus‐Organism‐Response Perspective ABSTRACT This study examined factors influencing Chinese college EFL learners’ intention to continue using AI‐based conversational agents for oral English practice. An integrated model combining technology affordance theory and the expectation‐confirmation model was established based on the S‐O‐R framework. Using 522 valid questionnaire responses, this study applied PLS‐SEM for data analysis. The results revealed that the three identified technology affordances served as external stimuli shaping learners' internal states, which in turn fostered their continuance intention. This work enriches relevant theories and offers practical insights. Theoretically, this study advances current knowledge by integrating technology affordances with post‐adoption psychology within a unified framework, thereby extending the theoretical boundaries of existing models. Practically, the findings provide guidance for AI developers to optimize user experience and for educators to integrate these tools into language learning environments.

title: Exploring Peer L2 Grit in Relation to Grit and Motivation
text_snippet: Exploring Peer L2 Grit in Relation to Grit and Motivation ABSTRACT Grit has attracted considerable attention because of its positive association with second language (L2) learning; however, its socio‐contextual dimensions remain underexplored. Specifically, little is known about how learners’ perceptions of their peers’ perseverance and sustained interest in L2 learning, conceptualized in this study as peer L2 grit, relate to their own L2 grit. This study examined L2 grit from socio‐contextual and motivational perspectives by focusing on peer L2 grit, domain‐general grit, and motivational types within self‐determination theory. Questionnaire data from undergraduate English learners in Japan ( N = 232) were analyzed using multiple regression analyses. Results show that both domain‐general and peer L2 grit are positively associated with L2 grit, with peer L2 grit showing a stronger relationship. In addition, both domain‐general and L2 grit are positively associated with autonomous motivation (i.e., intrinsic motivation and identified regulation), although these associations were stronger for L2 grit. Our findings highlight peer dynamics as an important socio‐contextual factor associated with L2 grit and underscore the importance of L2 grit in relation to high‐quality autonomous motivation in L2 learning.

title: The Effects of Gen‐AI on Situated and Future‐Driven Academic Writing Motivation
text_snippet: The Effects of Gen‐AI on Situated and Future‐Driven Academic Writing Motivation ABSTRACT Despite the increasing use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen‐AI) in education, there is still a significant gap in understanding its effects on the situated‐ and future‐driven motivation in academic writing. This longitudinal design‐based research sought to explore variations in academic writing motivation of 110 Chinese university English learners. It focused on two constructs: situated motivation, as conceptualised by self‐determination theory and future‐oriented motivation, through the L2 motivational self system. Data were collected at the beginning, middle and end of one semester through a combination of surveys, Motometer graphs, stimulated recall interviews and semi‐structured interviews. The analysis revealed three major findings. First, Gen‐AI use produced a significant change in identified regulation within situated motivation, while other components of situated motivation were not measurably affected. Second, Gen‐AI exerted a significant influence on future L2 selves within the future‐driven motivation. Third, the study underscores the critical role of basic psychological needs for autonomy and competence in bridging situated motivational experiences with the development of the ideal L2 self. Overall, the findings suggest that a pedagogically informed integration of Gen‐

title: Machine‐Translated Language as a Distinctive Translational Variety: Evidence From a Multivariate Analysis of Discourse Connectives Across Text Varieties and Genres
text_snippet: Machine‐Translated Language as a Distinctive Translational Variety: Evidence From a Multivariate Analysis of Discourse Connectives Across Text Varieties and Genres ABSTRACT Machine‐translated language is now produced and disseminated on an unprecedented scale, emerging as a new variety of translational language alongside human‐translated language. Yet its linguistic characteristics remain insufficiently understood. Focusing on discourse connectives, this study integrated exploratory correspondence analysis with confirmatory linear mixed‐effects modeling to examine the discourse‐level features of machine‐translated language. The results showed that: (1) machine‐translated language differed significantly from human‐produced language, including both human translations and human‐authored original texts, in academic abstracts and/or government documents, with machine‐translated texts favoring additive connectives and human‐produced texts favoring causal connectives, suggesting a contrast between safer, more general connective choices in machine outputs and more semantically specific discourse marking in human productions; (2) machine‐translated and human‐translated languages, both as varieties of translational language, used more additive connectives in government documents than human‐authored original texts, which showed higher frequencies of adversative and temporal connectives, r

title: Effects of Task Condition and Learner Proficiency on Syntactic Complexity in L2 Speech: Evidence From a Cross‐Sectional Learner Corpus
text_snippet: Effects of Task Condition and Learner Proficiency on Syntactic Complexity in L2 Speech: Evidence From a Cross‐Sectional Learner Corpus ABSTRACT While task effects on L2 speaking have been examined from a task‐based language teaching (TBLT) perspective, learner corpus research may offer a broader view of learner production and help address the problem of limited comparability of classroom‐ and lab‐based TBLT studies. This study explores the intersection of corpus linguistics and TBLT by investigating how task condition and learner proficiency influence syntactic complexity in L2 speech. Monologic and dialogic data from the International Corpus Network of Asian Learners of English were analyzed using the L2 Syntactic Complexity Analyzer. Findings revealed that the monologic task elicited more syntactically complex speech than the dialogic task. Syntactic complexity also increased with learner proficiency, particularly in the use of dependent clauses and complex nominals. Manual inspection of corpus data further revealed that dialogic tasks require negotiation for meaning, clarification requests, and confirmation checks. The results provide evidence of patterns associated with task conditions and proficiency in shaping L2 speech and inform both learner corpus compilation and L2 speaking task design.

title: An Investigation Into Resilience, Metacognition, and L2 Listening Comprehension
text_snippet: An Investigation Into Resilience, Metacognition, and L2 Listening Comprehension ABSTRACT Positive psychology in second language (L2) acquisition has increasingly attracted interest recently. Despite many studies highlighting the importance of resilience in L2 learning, a comprehensive understanding of its role in the skill‐specific domain of listening comprehension remains underdeveloped. This study aims to fill this gap by investigating the relationships among resilience, metacognition, and L2 listening comprehension in a cohort of 175 Chinese EFL high school students. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM), the study addressed two research questions regarding the structural paths among the three individual difference factors. Data were collected using a newly adapted Listening Resilience Scale, the Metacognitive Awareness Listening Questionnaire, and the Cambridge English A2 Key listening test. The results demonstrated that resilience significantly and positively influenced both metacognition and listening comprehension, and metacognition was a significant predictor of listening comprehension. Additionally, metacognition was found to partially mediate the relationship between resilience and L2 listening comprehension. These findings extend the application of resilience research from general language proficiency to skill‐specific domains, theoretica

title: From Feedback Appraisal to Pronunciation Performance: A Longitudinal Study of Learner Responses to Artificial Intelligence‐Based Pronunciation Feedback
text_snippet: From Feedback Appraisal to Pronunciation Performance: A Longitudinal Study of Learner Responses to Artificial Intelligence‐Based Pronunciation Feedback ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI)‐based pronunciation feedback is increasingly used in English as a foreign language learning, yet its pedagogical value depends not only on the delivery of automated feedback but also on how learners interpret, evaluate, and use such feedback in their pronunciation learning. Drawing on learner‐mediated perspectives on feedback processing, this study examined a baseline‐controlled longitudinal pathway linking perceived diagnosticity of AI pronunciation feedback, trust in AI pronunciation feedback, pronunciation self‐efficacy, and overall pronunciation performance. A two‐wave full‐panel longitudinal design was employed in a public college English course at a teacher education university in southwestern China. The participants were 790 first‐year students who regularly used FIF Oral English for after‐class pronunciation practice. Questionnaire data and teacher‐rated pronunciation performance were collected at both time points, with an interval of approximately ten weeks. Data were analyzed through reliability analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, longitudinal measurement invariance testing, and structural equation modeling with bootstrapped estimates of indirect associations. The results showe

title: Diving Into Language Teacher Beliefs: Experience and Contexts in Plurilingual Classrooms
text_snippet: Diving Into Language Teacher Beliefs: Experience and Contexts in Plurilingual Classrooms ABSTRACT This study investigates the pedagogical beliefs of French and English language teachers in a diverse, plurilingual context. Drawing on data from 57 pre‐service and in‐service teachers, it examines how beliefs vary according to teaching experience and target language (TL) taught in diverse educational settings. Data were collected through an online questionnaire and follow‐up focus groups. Questionnaire responses were analyzed descriptively and statistically, while focus group data underwent thematic coding. Overall, participants supported meaning‐oriented and communicative approaches, with openness to plurilingual strategies. Notable variations emerged: novice teachers were more receptive to learner‐centered and plurilingual practices, whereas experienced teachers favored a more balanced approach integrating form and meaning. Beliefs about pronunciation, reading, and the use of learners’ first languages also differed based on language taught and teaching context. These findings point to the importance of differentiated professional development that reflects teachers’ profiles and realities, recognizing the diverse beliefs they bring into increasingly plurilingual classrooms.

title: Negotiating Transnational Islamic Authority in Arabic Language Education: Teachers’ Practices in Indonesian Madrasahs
text_snippet: Negotiating Transnational Islamic Authority in Arabic Language Education: Teachers’ Practices in Indonesian Madrasahs ABSTRACT This study examines how Arabic language teachers in Indonesian madrasahs negotiate transnational Islamic authority and epistemic dependency within curriculum practices. Drawing on qualitative interviews, the research explores how global centres of Islamic knowledge—particularly Middle Eastern institutions, textbooks and linguistic norms—shape local understandings of legitimacy, authenticity and pedagogical authority. Rather than indicating structural domination, the findings show that epistemic dependency operates primarily as symbolic and referential alignment with perceived centres of authority. Teachers retain curricular autonomy and actively mediate these influences through contextual adaptation, aligning instruction with Indonesian cultural values, national educational frameworks and local religious traditions. These practices demonstrate negotiated forms of authority in which transnational standards function as reference points rather than mechanisms of control. The study contributes to discussions of language, curriculum and epistemic hierarchy in Global South contexts by highlighting how authority is symbolically structured yet locally mediated in practice.

title: Challenging the Monolith: Ambivalence, the Native‐Speaker Ideal and Teacher Preparation in Multilingual South Africa
text_snippet: Challenging the Monolith: Ambivalence, the Native‐Speaker Ideal and Teacher Preparation in Multilingual South Africa ABSTRACT This study explored the ambivalence of final‐year TESOL pre‐service teachers towards a non‐native‐speaking (NNS) lecturer within a historically white South African university. The research involved twelve student teachers being prepared to teach English as either a home language or a first additional language to high school learners in the Bachelor of Education programme. A significant factor was that this NNS English lecturer was the participants’ first such educator in their entire schooling history in English. I collected data using a focus group discussion, which was analysed thematically. The findings reveal a core tension in participant perceptions. Many openly valued the lecturer's empathy, metalinguistic knowledge and firsthand grasp of the local multilingual and superdiverse context. These views coexisted alongside deep‐seated native‐speakerist and racialised prejudices. For some, the lecturer's race and NNS status intersected uniquely, provoking unconscious challenges to their authority and expertise, presenting a stark contrast to the automatic acceptance granted white native‐speaking models. This conflict highlights how native‐speakerism functions not just as a linguistic bias but is also deeply infused with racial and social assumptions. The

title: The Relationship Among Motivational Disposition, Self‐Efficacy, and L2 Achievement of EFL Learners: A Regulatory Focus Theory Perspective
text_snippet: The Relationship Among Motivational Disposition, Self‐Efficacy, and L2 Achievement of EFL Learners: A Regulatory Focus Theory Perspective ABSTRACT Motivation has long been recognized as a crucial predictor of second language (L2) achievement, yet much existing research has treated motivation primarily in quantitative terms, with less attention to the nature of learners’ motivational orientations. Drawing on regulatory focus theory (RFT), this study examined how two distinct motivational dispositions (promotion focus vs. prevention focus) relate to L2 achievement, and whether English self‐efficacy mediates these relationships. A sample of 415 Chinese secondary EFL learners completed questionnaires measuring regulatory foci and English self‐efficacy, followed by an assessment of their L2 achievement. Structural equation modeling was employed to test the relationships among these variables. The results showed that (1) promotion focus positively predicted L2 achievement, while prevention focus negatively predicted L2 achievement; (2) promotion focus positively predicted self‐efficacy, while prevention focus negatively predicted self‐efficacy; and (3) self‐efficacy emerged as a significant mediator in the relationship between regulatory foci (promotion vs. prevention focus) and L2 achievement. title: Vocabulary Strategy Instruction in the Argentine EFL Context: Teachers’ Perspectives and Practices
text_snippet: Vocabulary Strategy Instruction in the Argentine EFL Context: Teachers’ Perspectives and Practices ABSTRACT Despite extensive research on vocabulary strategy instruction (VSI), little has been known about teachers’ perspectives on how it is understood and implemented in practice. This study investigated Argentinian EFL teachers’ priorities in vocabulary instruction, their perceived knowledge of learner strategies for spoken vocabulary, and factors contributing to their implementation of VSI. Adopting a sequential mixed‐methods design, questionnaire data were first collected from 83 in‐service Argentinian primary and secondary EFL teachers enrolled in a distance teacher education programme, followed by semi‐structured interviews with eight teachers from diverse institutional and teaching contexts. Quantitative findings showed a significant relationship between educational level and prioritised areas of vocabulary instruction among both primary and secondary teachers, particularly learner strategies for vocabulary comprehension, retention, and production. Teaching experience, prior experience with VSI, and school type were found to correlate with teachers’ perceived knowledge of VSI for spoken vocabulary. title: Form Without Function? Register Sensitivity in CEFR‐Conditioned LLM and Second‐Language Learner Writing
text_snippet: Form Without Function? Register Sensitivity in CEFR‐Conditioned LLM and Second‐Language Learner Writing ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) can generate text that resembles L2 learner writing at requested proficiency levels, but whether such texts adapt to communicative contexts as human learners do remains unclear. This study compared LLM‐generated and human second‐language writing across three task‐defined categories (informal–personal, semi‐formal–expository, formal–argumentative) and four CEFR levels (A2–C1) using Biber's multi‐dimensional analysis (MDA). Six instruction‐tuned models responded to Write & Improve prompts ( n = 592 human; n = 4724 LLM), with EFCAMDAT as a human baseline. Under CEFR‐only prompting, LLM outputs shifted on MDA dimensions tied to informational density and explicitness, but showed weaker, differently directed, or less variable differentiation on dimensions tied to persuasion and elaboration, especially in formal–argumentative tasks. The largest observed gap was at C1, where CEFR descriptors most emphasize register flexibility. LLM outputs were more uniform than human writing and clustered near the center of the human distributional space, showing less variation than authentic learner texts. title: A Critical Visual Analysis of Moral Values Representation in Chinese Primary School English Textbooks: A Visual Grammar Perspective
text_snippet: A Critical Visual Analysis of Moral Values Representation in Chinese Primary School English Textbooks: A Visual Grammar Perspective ABSTRACT This study investigates the distribution and visual representation of moral values in a series of Chinese primary school English textbooks. The results identify eight core moral values. While the distribution generally aligns with the developmental characteristics of children's cognitive abilities, certain key values are underrepresented, leading to an imbalance. By adopting Kress and van Leeuwen's visual grammar theory, the study explores representational, interactive, and compositional meanings constructed through visual resources in the textbooks. It is concluded that these visual resources effectively complement textual content in conveying moral values. Finally, practical implications for textbook developers, illustrators, and teachers are put forward.

title: Giving a Voice to Survivors: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Women's Narratives of Sexual Violence
text_snippet: Giving a Voice to Survivors: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Women's Narratives of Sexual Violence ABSTRACT Sexual violence constitutes a pervasive global issue, disproportionately affecting women and girls and resulting in serious health consequences, making it essential to give a voice to survivors. This study employed the transitivity model to analyse the discourse of women survivors, focusing on how they recount and interpret their experiences, alongside quantitative data on their perceptions of severity and risk. Results from the discourse analysis showed that mental processes were most frequent (32%), reflecting a discussion of thoughts, feelings, desires and perceptions, followed by relational processes (26.8%), material processes (25%) and verbal processes (14.2%); meanwhile, behavioural and existential processes were rare (1% each). Quantitative findings indicated that participants reported a higher perceived severity of violence and greater risk to their lives retrospectively than at the time of the incidents. Trauma‐informed approaches that validate survivors’ perceptions, emotions and meaning‐making processes are, therefore, essential.

title: Keeping Learners in the Optimal Challenge Zone: Generative AI–Based Task Personalization in College EFL Classes
text_snippet: Keeping Learners in the Optimal Challenge Zone: Generative AI–Based Task Personalization in College EFL Classes ABSTRACT In college English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classes, a mismatch between task complexity and learners’ speaking skills can reduce engagement and limit learning outcomes. To address the difficulty of implementing differentiated task grading in large‐scale classrooms, this study introduces generative AI (GenAI) as the control center and examines the personalized task complexity regulation mechanism based on learners’ immediate performance and emotional feedback. The study adopted a 10‐week quasi‐experimental design. A total of 70 first‐year undergraduate students from a university in western China participated in the study, with 35 students assigned to the experimental group and 35 to the control group. Both groups completed multiple rounds of speaking tasks under the same conditions and with the same communication goals. After each round, the experimental group collected data on complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF), self‐assessed task difficulty, and anxiety, and adjusted the complexity of subsequent tasks accordingly. The control group increased the difficulty in a preset uniform sequence. title: Self‐Directed Teaching Strategies and Professional Learning in Technological Implementation: A Collaborative Autoethnography
text_snippet: Self‐Directed Teaching Strategies and Professional Learning in Technological Implementation: A Collaborative Autoethnography ABSTRACT Technological integration into teaching offers significant pedagogical potential, yet it can also intensify the challenge of addressing systemic barriers to inclusion. This issue is especially important for teaching‐focused academics (TAs), who are increasingly leading classroom instruction and translating institutional digital priorities into inclusive classroom practice in higher education. However, their experiences of self‐directing technology integration, differentiating instruction for diverse learners and aligning with their professional learning (PL) goals are underrepresented, insufficiently recognised and generally framed from deficit‐based rather than expertise‐based perspectives. Addressing this gap, this study examines the collaborative professional narratives of two experienced TAs teaching two shared TESOL postgraduate courses at a leading Australian university. Employing collaborative autoethnography (CAE) as an insider‐oriented methodology, in light of a recently modified technological, affective, pedagogical and content knowledge (TAPACK) model, this CAE illustrates how self‐directed strategies support inclusive, technology‐mediated learning for CALD students. title: The Effect of Task Complexity on Second Language Writing Performance Between Computer‐Assisted Individual and Collaborative Writing
text_snippet: The Effect of Task Complexity on Second Language Writing Performance Between Computer‐Assisted Individual and Collaborative Writing ABSTRACT This study explored the extent to which the effect of task complexity on writing performance would differ between computer‐assisted individual versus collaborative writing. Participants were 112 Chinese users of English as a second language. They completed two reading‐to‐write tasks of varying cognitive complexity either individually ( n = 56) or collaboratively ( n = 56). Task complexity was manipulated as the presence or absence of a text structure for summary writing. The resulting texts were analyzed for linguistic complexity, accuracy, and text quality. It was found that the effects of task complexity on the use of academic words and phrasal structures, as well as the analytic rating of organization, differed between individual and collaborative writing. In individual writing, no significant differences were observed in these measures between the simple and complex tasks. In contrast, higher levels of performance were observed in the simple task in collaborative writing. These findings suggest that collaborative writing may play a more beneficial role than individual writing in text production.

title: Profile of EFL Learners’ AI‐Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English, Digital Nativity, Desire, and Online Self‐Efficacy: Associations With Demographic Features
text_snippet: Profile of EFL Learners’ AI‐Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English, Digital Nativity, Desire, and Online Self‐Efficacy: Associations With Demographic Features ABSTRACT This study examines the profiles of learners of English as a foreign language within AI‐mediated informal digital learning of English (IDLE) environments, emphasizing AI‐mediated IDLE, digital nativity, desire, and online self‐efficacy, as well as their correlations with demographic characteristics. Using latent profile analysis (LPA), 1994 Chinese university students were categorized into three profiles: versatile digital natives, selective digital navigators, and emerging digital natives. Versatile digital natives showed high engagement in AI‐mediated IDLE activities, a strong desire for English learning, and robust online self‐efficacy. Selective digital navigators preferred structured and receptive IDLE activities, showing moderate desire and self‐efficacy. In contrast, emerging digital natives had lower engagement and digital proficiency, but they showed potential in interactive activities. Significant differences were found across profiles in terms of gender, digital device duration, and frequency of AI‐mediated IDLE use, and location, but not in age, using the R3STEP command. The findings highlight the need for tailored educational strategies to support diverse learner profiles, thereby enhancing la

title: Learner Agency Priorities and Speaking Performance in GenAI‐Mediated Project‐Based Learning (PBL): Evidence From Q Methodology
text_snippet: Learner Agency Priorities and Speaking Performance in GenAI‐Mediated Project‐Based Learning (PBL): Evidence From Q Methodology ABSTRACT Project‐based learning (PBL) is widely used in foreign language education to organise learning around sustained collaboration and tangible outcomes, yet little is known about how learners prioritise agency‐related behaviours in PBL speaking tasks when generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are available during project work. To address this gap, this study used Q methodology with 49 Chinese undergraduates in a Chinese university English course to examine two questions: (1) What distinct learner agency priorities emerge in GenAI‐mediated PBL? and (2) How are these priorities associated with differences in learners’ speaking performance? Participants completed Q‐sorts that required them to rank agency‐related statements and by‐person factor analysis was used to identify shared learner agency viewpoints. Persuasive speech ratings were then compared across the resulting viewpoint groups to examine whether different agency‐priority patterns were associated with variation in speaking performance. Three viewpoints were extracted, foregrounding strategy use with GenAI, personal beliefs and motivation and teamwork in GenAI‐mediated project work. title: When Knowing Is Not Enough: EFL Teachers’ Knowledge, Self‐Efficacy and Professional Development in Critical Thinking Instruction
text_snippet: When Knowing Is Not Enough: EFL Teachers’ Knowledge, Self‐Efficacy and Professional Development in Critical Thinking Instruction ABSTRACT Critical thinking (CT) is increasingly recognised as a vital educational goal, yet little is known about how EFL teachers conceptualise CT and develop confidence in teaching it. This study investigated how Japanese high school EFL teachers made sense of CT and what shapes their self‐efficacy for CT instruction. Using teacher language awareness as an interpretive lens, this study combined an online survey ( N = 82) with follow‐up interviews ( N = 17). Findings suggested that teachers recognised key elements of CT, but their conceptions were often partial. Overall self‐efficacy was moderate: teachers felt comparatively confident in diagnosing and explaining students’ CT‐related difficulties, but less confident in promoting CT more broadly or strengthening students’ confidence. Self‐efficacy appeared to be shaped more by prior experiences and anticipated student reactions than by CT knowledge alone. These results point to a disjunction between teachers’ knowledge and confidence, highlighting a need for professional development that supports a fuller understanding of CT and its scaffolded enactment through classroom language practices. title: Exploring the Role of AI in EFL Students’ Autonomy, Relatedness, and Competence Through the Lens of Self‐Determination Theory (SDT): A Latent Growth Curve Modeling (LGCM) Analysis
text_snippet: Exploring the Role of AI in EFL Students’ Autonomy, Relatedness, and Competence Through the Lens of Self‐Determination Theory (SDT): A Latent Growth Curve Modeling (LGCM) Analysis ABSTRACT A growing body of research has reported the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on different areas of second/foreign language (L2) education in recent years. However, there is insufficient research on the role of AI‐mediated L2 education in the fluctuations and changes of learner‐related factors in English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts. Moreover, the interaction of learning theories and AI integration has also been overlooked. To fill these gaps, this study drew on self‐determination theory (SDT) to examine the changes in students’ autonomy, relatedness, and competence over three time periods. To do so, 595 Chinese EFL students were non‐randomly selected to complete a survey at the outset, middle, and end of an AI‐powered L2 education course. In line with the specified goals, latent growth curve modeling (LGCM) was used to inspect developmental trajectories and fluctuations. The results revealed that, over the three time periods, EFL students’ autonomy, relatedness, and competence developed in light of the introduction of AI technologies. title: Exploring the Impact of AI‐Driven Writing Tutor Chatbots on Adolescent L2 Writers’ Revision and Editing: A Complexity, Cohesion, and Accuracy Analysis
text_snippet: Exploring the Impact of AI‐Driven Writing Tutor Chatbots on Adolescent L2 Writers’ Revision and Editing: A Complexity, Cohesion, and Accuracy Analysis ABSTRACT This study investigates how AI‐driven writing tutor chatbots influence adolescent L2 writers’ revision and editing during process writing, focusing on the effects on linguistic complexity, cohesion, and accuracy. A total of 71 Korean middle school English learners revised and edited their drafts with the assistance of stage‐specific chatbots across two genres: expository and argumentative essays. The impact of the chatbots was analyzed according to each stage of the writing process. During revision, changes in lexical and lexicogrammatical complexity and cohesive features were examined; during editing, changes in grammatical and mechanical accuracy were assessed. The findings revealed that the writing tutor chatbots effectively supported learners’ revision and editing, resulting in notable improvements across targeted dimensions of complexity, cohesion, and accuracy. Furthermore, genre‐specific differences were observed, suggesting that the chatbots’ effects may vary depending on the rhetorical and linguistic demands of each genre. The study provides pedagogical insights for integrating AI chatbots into process‐oriented writing instruction for L2 learners.

title: Propositional Density in EFL Retellings: Relative Contributions of Proficiency, Speech Rate, Lexical Diversity, and Mean Dependency Distance
text_snippet: Propositional Density in EFL Retellings: Relative Contributions of Proficiency, Speech Rate, Lexical Diversity, and Mean Dependency Distance ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between form and meaning in text recall by examining how linguistic factors—EFL proficiency, speech rate, lexical diversity, and mean dependency distance (MDD)—contribute to propositional density (PD) in 140 EFL learners’ retellings. Propositions were classified into two categories: those identical to the auditory input and those idiosyncratic to the learners’ output. Path analysis revealed that the model accounted for 29% of the variance in identical PD and 30% in idiosyncratic PD. While EFL proficiency emerged as the predominant predictor of identical PD, MDD exerted the strongest positive influence on idiosyncratic PD. Speech rate and lexical diversity moderately predicted identical PD. Although speech rate significantly mediated the indirect effect of EFL proficiency on PD, lexical diversity and MDD showed no such mediating effects. These findings suggest a functional shift: while proficiency and speech rate correlate directly with verbatim repetition, syntactic complexity—measured by MDD—is the dominant positive predictor of conceptual reconstruction. This study highlights the complex interplay between form and meaning construction in EFL oral production.

title: Unpacking the Impact of L2 Motivation on Intended Effort Among Chinese Tertiary EFL Learners: Chain Mediating Roles of Use of Mediational Resources and Demotivation
text_snippet: Unpacking the Impact of L2 Motivation on Intended Effort Among Chinese Tertiary EFL Learners: Chain Mediating Roles of Use of Mediational Resources and Demotivation ABSTRACT While studies have explored the effect of second language (L2) motivation on intended effort, research investigating how demotivation and the use of mediational resources mediate the relationship between L2 motivation and intended effort remains scarce. To address this gap, the present study aims to explore the mediating roles of demotivation and the use of mediational resources between L2 motivation and intended effort. Data were collected via a questionnaire survey administered to 1149 Chinese tertiary English as a foreign language (EFL) learners and analysed using SPSS 26.0 and AMOS 28.0. The results indicate that L2 motivation significantly and positively predicts learners’ intended effort; L2 motivation negatively predicts demotivation and positively predicts the use of mediational resources; the use of mediational resources and demotivation play a chain mediating role in linking L2 motivation and intended effort. This study elucidates the mediating mechanism of the use of mediational resources and demotivation in the relationship between L2 motivation and intended effort. It transcends the traditional paradigm that focuses on a single variable or direct effects alone, providing a systemic explanation

title: English Pronunciation Teaching at Secondary Schools: Discoveries From an EFL Context
text_snippet: English Pronunciation Teaching at Secondary Schools: Discoveries From an EFL Context ABSTRACT Pronunciation research within the past three decades has seen growing empirical evidence on the efficiency of deliberate, explicit phonetic instruction on second language learners’ intelligibility and/or comprehensibility. This body of work has also examined how pronunciation is represented in instructional materials, how teachers construct pronunciation teaching and what pedagogic beliefs they hold, and how students perceive pronunciation instruction. To date, however, research on EFL teachers’ pronunciation teaching at secondary schools and how this particular cohort of teachers learn to teach pronunciation is relatively limited. The present study addresses this research gap by investigating Vietnamese secondary EFL teachers’ pronunciation teaching practices, what pedagogic beliefs shaped their instruction, and what kind of pronunciation pedagogy training they received. Qualitative data were collected from written reflections, classroom observations, and individual interviews with nine teachers of English across three secondary schools in South Vietnam. Findings reveal that the teachers’ pronunciation teaching mainly centered on: (1) repetition drills, (2) corrective feedback through recasts and/or prompts, and (3) Vietnamese transcriptions, with repetition drills being the most comm

title: AI‐Supported Socratic Dialogue Agents vs. Generic AI Chatbots for Intermediate EFL Learners’ Critical Thinking, Epistemic Beliefs, and Argumentation: Mixed‐Methods Evidence
text_snippet: AI‐Supported Socratic Dialogue Agents vs. Generic AI Chatbots for Intermediate EFL Learners’ Critical Thinking, Epistemic Beliefs, and Argumentation: Mixed‐Methods Evidence ABSTRACT This mixed‐methods, quasi‐experimental study investigated the impact of artificial intelligence (AI)‐supported Socratic Dialogue Agents (SDAs) on critical thinking, epistemic beliefs, and argumentation skills among intermediate English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. Ninety male intermediate EFL learners from Iranian language institutes were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (a) an AI‐Socratic dialogue agent group, (b) a generic AI chatbot group, or (c) a no‐AI control group. Quantitative data were collected through validated instruments before and after the intervention and then analyzed using mixed‐design analyses of variance (ANOVAs). To complement these results, qualitative data from post‐intervention focus groups (five participants per group) were examined through thematic analysis to elicit perceptions and through content‐structural analysis to examine real‐time English interactions. title: Unraveling Effects of Digital Personalized Vocabulary Learning: An Evidence‐Based Analysis From Four‐Dimensional Theory
text_snippet: Unraveling Effects of Digital Personalized Vocabulary Learning: An Evidence‐Based Analysis From Four‐Dimensional Theory ABSTRACT Although digital personalized vocabulary learning (DPVL) tools have become widespread innovations, a thorough evaluation of its effectiveness in English as a foreign language (EFL) vocabulary learning has been notably absent. This research aimed to achieve a deeper insight into the overall and moderating effects by employing a four‐dimensional perspective on personalization, conducting a meta‐analysis that encompassed 25 effect sizes on DPVL published from 2004 to 2024 with 1342 EFL learners. The results highlighted that (a) DPVL produces significant improved learning gains compared to a diverse range of non‐personalized vocabulary instruction, including paper‐based learning, conventional classroom instruction, and non‐personalized digital learning, demonstrating a moderate‐to‐large effect of g = 0.761; and (b) different age groups, system types, and intervention durations play a moderating role in the effects of DPVL. Inspired by the research results, some implications for future academic explorations were proposed as well.

title: Beyond Compartmentalized L1/L2 Teaching: Connecting Languages to Foster In‐Depth Learning and Multi/Trans Lingual Selves
text_snippet: Beyond Compartmentalized L1/L2 Teaching: Connecting Languages to Foster In‐Depth Learning and Multi/Trans Lingual Selves ABSTRACT This paper examines elementary Grade 5 and 6 students’ emic perspectives on their L1 French and L2 English teachers’ cross‐curricular efforts to build linguistic and conceptual bridges. Drawing on research on translanguaging pedagogies and recent motivation scholarship, we propose a multi‐competence view of motivation that aligns more closely with translanguaging classroom practices. Using this lens, we analyzed focal students’ interview data on their linguistic profiles, aspirations for language learning and use, and perceptions of teachers’ attempts to integrate the two school languages while encouraging them to draw on their entire repertoires for meaning making. Findings show that students sought to affirm, mobilize, and expand their desired multi/translingual selves for present and future purposes. Teachers’ translanguaging approaches not only supported comprehension and vocabulary development but, crucially, aligned with students’ aspired multi/translingual identities. We argue that such dynamic pedagogies can enhance motivation and investment beyond a single target language, calling for a reconceptualization of motivation theories to recognize the interdependent, shifting dynamics across learners’ multilingual motivational systems.

title: Exploring the Integration of Artificial Intelligence in EFL Teaching: Teachers' Perspectives and Practices in Poland
text_snippet: Exploring the Integration of Artificial Intelligence in EFL Teaching: Teachers' Perspectives and Practices in Poland ABSTRACT This study investigates how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers in Poland integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into their teaching and how they evaluate its pedagogical value. Drawing on data from a nationwide survey of 358 EFL teachers across educational levels and regions, the study examines patterns of AI use and explores teachers’ perceptions across four interrelated dimensions: perceived benefits and challenges, self‐assessed competence and training, and views on AI's long‐term implications for the teaching profession. The findings indicate that AI‐based tools are widely employed for instructional purposes, particularly for material development and language practice, whereas their use for assessment and administrative tasks remains limited. Teachers generally acknowledge the potential of generative technologies to support instruction and personalize learning; however, they also express substantial concerns regarding academic integrity, students’ cognitive engagement, and ethical implementation. Although respondents largely reject the notion that intelligent applications could replace human educators, many report limited preparedness to integrate them confidently due to insufficient training and institutional support.
